lead: The week after Aneede Sunday, the last week before the Great Fast, opens with prayer. In Colossians, Paul tells a young Church what he asks God to give it. In Matthew, Jesus gives his disciples the words to ask with. The two readings share more than a subject: both speak of the kingdom, both speak of forgiveness, and both use the same Greek verb for God's rescue of us.

set: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley, in what is now south-western Turkey. Paul did not found the Church there. It learned the gospel from Epaphras (1:7), and it seems that many there had never seen Paul's face (2:1). The letter names Paul and Timothy as its senders (1:1). Many scholars think a disciple wrote it in Paul's name, while others hold it to be his own; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.
These verses follow the thanksgiving of 1:3–8 and run straight into the great hymn to Christ (1:15–20). The closing words about the “beloved Son” are the bridge to that hymn.
str: vv. 9–10: what Paul asks for: a knowledge of God's will that turns into a way of life.
v. 11: strength, and the patience to endure.
v. 12: thanks to the Father for a share in the inheritance.
vv. 13–14: the reason for the thanks: rescue, transfer, redemption.
kw: A fuller word than plain knowing. It is not knowledge for its own sake: in v. 10 it is both the root and the fruit of a good life.

The verb means to move someone from one place to another, and writers of the time also used it for moving whole populations. Paul pictures the baptized as a people resettled from one realm to another.
Literally a release on payment, the word used of setting captives at liberty. Here Paul explains it himself: “the forgiveness of sins”.
vv: so that you may lead lives worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing to him, as you bear fruit in every good work and as you grow in the knowledge of God.
Knowing God and doing good feed each other. The verse does not let us choose between a Church that studies and a Church that serves.
He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son,

Both verbs are in the past tense. Paul does not say that God will one day do this, but that he has done it. The verb for “rescued” (rhyomai) is the one used in the last petition of the Lord's Prayer in today's Gospel.
in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
The kingdom of the Son is not first a territory. It is a place where sins are forgiven, and we are in it “in him”.
ch: The Catechism cites these verses when it says that Christ's whole life is a mystery of redemption (CCC 517). It also uses them when it teaches why even children need Baptism: every person born into our fallen state needs to be delivered from the power of darkness and brought into the realm of the children of God (CCC 1250). Each baptism in the parish is this verse happening again.

set: The Lord's Prayer stands near the middle of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), in a section on almsgiving, prayer and fasting done for the Father “who sees in secret” (6:1–18). Luke gives a shorter form (Luke 11:2–4); the Catechism notes that Luke has five petitions and Matthew seven, and that the Church's liturgy follows Matthew's (CCC 2759).

Jesus prays here as a son of Israel. Its first petitions are close in spirit to Jewish prayers such as the Kaddish, though we know that prayer only from later texts. Very early the Christians made it their daily prayer: the Didache, a Church manual probably from around the end of the first century, tells them to pray it three times a day (Didache 8).
str: v. 9a: the address: “Our Father in heaven”.
vv. 9b–10: three petitions about God: his name, his kingdom, his will.
vv. 11–13: four petitions about us: bread, forgiveness, testing, rescue.
vv. 14–15: a comment on one petition only, forgiveness.
kw: A puzzle. Origen already remarked that the word was not known to him from other Greek writers. It may mean “for today”, “for tomorrow” or “needed for existence”. The Catechism holds the senses together: bread for this day, and, taken literally, “super-essential” bread, the Bread of Life (CCC 2837).

Matthew writes “debts”; Luke 11:4 writes “sins”. In the Aramaic that Jesus spoke, and in the Syriac Bible of our own tradition (ḥawbā), the same word means both a debt and a sin. Sin leaves us owing something we cannot repay.
A test or a trial, and also a temptation. The word can look to the daily struggle and to the great final trial as well.
vv: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.

“Our”, not “my”. Nobody can say this prayer alone, even in an empty room. To hallow the name is to know it as holy and to treat it so. As a petition, it draws both God and us into the work (CCC 2807).
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

This is the only petition with a condition attached, and the only one that Jesus comments on afterwards (vv. 14–15). The Catechism is realistic about it: we cannot make ourselves stop feeling a hurt or forget it, but a heart given to the Holy Spirit can turn the injury into compassion (CCC 2843).
And do not bring us to the time of trial, but rescue us from the evil one.

A note on the text. The oldest Greek manuscripts end here. The closing “for the kingdom and the power and the glory” is found in later manuscripts, and a form of it is already in the Didache. It grew from the Church's praying of this prayer, and the Eastern liturgies use it.
ch: Tertullian called this prayer “truly the summary of the whole gospel”, and St Augustine said that every prayer of Scripture is found in it (in substance; CCC 2761–2762). The Catechism closes its whole teaching on prayer with a commentary on it (CCC 2759–2865). In the Holy Qurbono we say it just before Communion: we ask for daily bread and forgiveness at the moment we are about to receive the Bread of Life with our neighbour beside us.

qa: Does God lead us into temptation?

No. “God cannot be tempted by evil and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13). The Catechism explains that the Greek idea behind the petition includes both “do not let us enter into temptation” and “do not let us give way to it” (CCC 2846). We are asking the Father to hold on to us in the hour of testing.
study: Paul prays that the Colossians may grow in knowledge and in good works together. Which of the two do I find harder to keep alive?
Is there one person whose name makes “as we also have forgiven” hard to say? What would it mean to bring that difficulty honestly to the Father before receiving Communion?

lead: Mayaltho, the Entrance of our Lord into the Temple, falls on the fortieth day from Yaldo, counting the feast itself. A poor young couple climb to Jerusalem to do what the Law asks, and with them the Lord enters his own house, carried in his mother's arms. “The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple” (Malachi 3:1).

The lectionary is rich today. The Old Testament lessons give the law of offerings without blemish (Leviticus 22:17–25: “to be acceptable it must be perfect”, 22:21), the anointing of David at Hebron (2 Samuel 5:1–5), and the promise that “a shoot shall come out from the stump of Jesse” (Isaiah 11:1). In Acts, Paul stands before the governor Felix and confesses his hope in the resurrection (Acts 24:14–21). The Evening Gospel tells the whole scene in the Temple (Luke 2:22–35), and the Gospel of the Holy Qurbono takes up its opening verses (Luke 2:22–24).

Three readings are studied here. Leviticus gives the law that brought Mary and Joseph to the Temple. Hebrews shows the true sanctuary that the Child will one day enter. Luke, studied as one passage with the Evening Gospel, shows the meeting at the door. The key words of this feast are offering, entrance and light.

r.h: The offering of a poor mother
set: Of the Old Testament lessons this one stands closest to the Gospel: it is the very law Luke has in mind. Leviticus 11–15 sets out what made a person ritually clean or unclean, that is, fit or not fit to come near the sanctuary. Chapter 12 is a short law for a mother after childbirth.

This is the language of worship, not of guilt. Israel treated the great mysteries of life and death, above all blood, as things that set a person apart for a time. The first blessing of Scripture is “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28), and nothing in this chapter calls birth a sin.
str: vv. 1–4: a son: seven days of uncleanness, circumcision on the eighth day, then thirty-three days of purification.
v. 5: a daughter: the periods are doubled, to two weeks and sixty-six days. The text gives no reason.
vv. 6–7: the offering at the end: a lamb and a bird.
v. 8: the mercy clause for those who cannot afford a lamb.
¶ Seven and thirty-three make forty days. This is why the Lord's entrance into the Temple is kept forty days after his birth.
kw: A ritual state, not a moral fault. It kept a person for a time from holy things (v. 4). It ended by the passing of time and an offering.
The usual translation, but many scholars prefer “purification offering”, since here, as in other places in Leviticus, no sin has been committed. The rite restores a person's access to the sanctuary.
The priest's act in vv. 7–8. The root meaning is debated: to cover, or to wipe clean. It is the verb behind Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.
vv: Her time of blood purification shall be thirty-three days; she shall not touch any holy thing, or come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purification are completed.
The aim of the waiting is the return. The law looks forward to the day the mother comes back to the sanctuary and stands before God again.
If she cannot afford a sheep, she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons,

A small verse of great mercy. God's law makes room for the poor, and the poor woman's offering is received as fully as a rich woman's. Luke will quote exactly this provision for Mary. She did not bring a lamb.
ch: St Paul writes that God sent his Son “born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). Mary and Joseph keep this law to the letter. The Second Vatican Council notes that when Mary presented her Son in the Temple she made “the offering of the poor” (Lumen Gentium 57). Preachers have long remarked that the mother who brought two birds was carrying the Lamb in her arms.

set: Our lectionary reads this as an “Epistle of St Paul”, following the old custom of receiving Hebrews with his letters, though the letter itself does not name its author. It calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). It seems to be a sermon for Christians, perhaps of Jewish background, who had grown tired.

Just before this passage the writer has described the earthly tent and the Day of Atonement, when the high priest entered the inner room once a year with blood (9:1–10; Leviticus 16). Today's verses set Christ's entry beside it. On this feast the Child enters the Temple of stone, carried by others. Hebrews looks ahead to the day he will enter the true sanctuary by his own act.
str: vv. 11–12: the entry of Christ: through a greater tent, with his own blood, once for all.
vv. 13–14: an argument from the lesser to the greater: “how much more”.
kw: The high priest had to return every year. Christ's offering is never repeated, because nothing is lacking to it.
The release of a captive or a slave at a price. In Luke 2:38, a verse just beyond this feast's reading, Anna speaks to those waiting for the same thing: the redemption of Jerusalem.
The word the Greek Old Testament uses for an animal fit for sacrifice. Leviticus 22, also read today, asks for offerings without blemish. Here the phrase describes a person who gives himself.
vv: But when Christ came as a high priest of the good things that have come,

A note on the text. Some of the oldest manuscripts read “the good things that have come”, which the NRSV follows. Many others, and the Latin Vulgate, read “the good things to come”, which the Malayalam POC follows. Both are true to the faith: in Christ the good things have come, and their fullness is still ahead.
he entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption.
The Child on whose behalf two birds are offered today is himself the offering to come. The parents' gift at the Temple door points to the gift he will make when he has grown.
how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to worship the living God!
Ritual purity touched the body, as this verse's neighbour says (v. 13). Christ reaches the conscience. The goal is not only that we be clean, but that we may worship.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ entered heaven itself as our high priest (CCC 662), and that the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the Cross and does not add another (CCC 1366–1367). St John Chrysostom, preaching on Hebrews, says that we do not offer another sacrifice each day but always the same one (in substance). So each Holy Qurbono is an entrance: with Christ the Church goes in where he has gone.

r.h: My eyes have seen your salvation
set: Luke opens and closes his infancy story in the Temple (1:5–23; 2:41–51), and he shows a family obedient to the Law; he mentions the Law five times in this chapter (2:22, 23, 24, 27, 39). He brings two laws together. A mother was to be purified (Leviticus 12). A firstborn son belonged to the Lord (Exodus 13:2) and was to be redeemed (Numbers 18:15–16). Luke mentions no payment. Instead he says that they came “to present him to the Lord”, which recalls Hannah bringing Samuel to the sanctuary (1 Samuel 1:24–28).

The Gospel of the day, vv. 22–24, gives the family's obedience; the Evening Gospel continues with the meeting. The people who meet here are not the powerful. Simeon holds no office that Luke mentions. He is known only for his waiting.
str: vv. 22–24: the parents fulfil the Law and bring the offering of the poor.
vv. 25–28: Simeon, moved by the Spirit, comes to the Temple and takes the child.
vv. 29–32: his song, the Nunc Dimittis.
vv. 33–35: the parents' amazement, and the word to Mary.
kw: A word for placing someone before a higher person. It can also be used for bringing an offering. Luke chooses it for a child brought before God. Paul uses it when he asks us to present our bodies as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1).
The word for releasing a servant. Simeon calls God “Master” (despotēs) and himself a servant. He is a watchman who may now go off duty.
Literally “spoken against”. The child brings peace, and he also brings a decision, for the same light that comforts also exposes. The Malayalam POC gives “വിവാദവിഷയമായ അടയാളം”.
vv: they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord
The child is already the Lord's, and they bring him there in obedience. Every Christian parent at a font does something similar: a child who belongs to God is given back to God.
and they offered a sacrifice according to what is stated in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”
This is the provision of Leviticus 12:8 for those who could not afford a lamb. Luke, without any comment, shows us the economic state of the Holy Family.
“Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word;
The long wait ends in peace, because the promise has been kept. The song weaves together phrases from the second part of Isaiah, which spoke to the exiles.
for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.”

Simeon is looking at a baby, and he speaks of all the peoples. Isaiah's servant is “a light to the nations” (Isaiah 49:6). The two halves of the verse belong together: the light for the Gentiles does not take away the glory of Israel.
and a sword will pierce your own soul too.”
The first shadow of the Cross in Luke falls on the mother. Joy and sorrow stand at the same door of the Temple.
ch: The Catechism says the Presentation shows Jesus to be the firstborn Son who belongs to the Lord. In Simeon and Anna all Israel comes to meet its Saviour, and the sword foretold for Mary announces Christ's one offering on the Cross (CCC 529). Jesus was presented in the Temple forty days after his birth, and he always kept a deep respect for it (CCC 583). The feast was already kept solemnly in Jerusalem in the fourth century, as the pilgrim Egeria records. St Sophronius of Jerusalem invites all the faithful to go out with lights to meet the Lord and to embrace him as Simeon did (in substance).

qa: Did Mary need to be purified?

No. The Church believes that Mary was preserved from all sin (CCC 411, 493), and that Christ's birth did not diminish her virginal integrity but sanctified it (CCC 499). Ritual uncleanness in any case was not a sin. She kept the law as her Son did, for he too was “born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). A small detail of the text: the Greek of Luke 2:22 says “their purification”, while the Latin Vulgate says “her purification”. Scholars explain this in different ways. Luke may be thinking of the whole family going up together.
Why did the law set a longer time after the birth of a daughter?

Leviticus does not say. Jewish and Christian interpreters have offered various reasons, and none is certain. We should not read a lower dignity into it: the same offering is asked for a son or a daughter (12:6), and Scripture says from its first page that man and woman alike are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27; CCC 369).
What is the sword that pierces Mary's soul?

Some early writers, Origen among them, thought of a moment of doubt at the Cross. The settled reading of the Church is sorrow: Mary stands by the Cross and shares in her Son's suffering (John 19:25–27). The Catechism reads Simeon's word as announcing Christ's perfect offering on the Cross (CCC 529), and the Council speaks of her uniting herself with his sacrifice (Lumen Gentium 58).
rite: The Syriac name Mayaltho means entrance, and the feast looks to the Lord himself: he comes in, and his people go out to meet him. St Ephrem, in his Homily on our Lord, calls Simeon a priest and sees a surprising exchange: Simeon thought he was presenting the child to God, while it was the child who was presenting Simeon to his Lord (in substance). Mayaltho stands at the threshold of the Great Fast. Before we set out on the long road to Qyomtho, we are shown where the road ends, in the arms of a God who keeps his word. In the Holy Qurbono we too receive him, and we may go in peace.
study: Leviticus 12:8 makes room for the poor at God's altar. Who in my parish might feel that they have too little to bring? How do we make room for them?
Hebrews 9:14 says the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience “to worship the living God”. What “dead works” should I bring to him before this Great Fast?
Simeon's whole life was a waiting. What have I stopped waiting for from God?
Mary hears of a sword while she holds a child. How can joy and sorrow live together in a Christian life, and in my own family?

lead: Our Church today keeps close to the Temple door and remembers Mar Shem'on and Morth Hanna, Simeon and Anna. Luke shows us two people whose long years of prayer end in a meeting. Paul's prayer in Ephesians shows what such a life is rooted in. Together the readings teach that the Holy Spirit does much of his work slowly, in those who stay faithful.

set: This prayer closes the first half of the letter. Chapters 1–3 tell what God has done in Christ, bringing Jew and Gentile into one body; chapters 4–6 tell how to live because of it. The letter names Paul as its author, though many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.
str: vv. 14–15: Paul kneels before the Father.
vv. 16–17: he asks for inner strength and for Christ to dwell in the heart.
vv. 18–19: he asks that they may know a love beyond knowing.
vv. 20–21: a song of praise to the God who can do more than we ask.
kw: A wordplay on patēr, “Father”: every patria takes its name from the patēr. The POC brings this out with പിതൃത്വങ്ങൾ. All belonging begins in him.
To settle in a house and live there, not to visit. Paul prays that Christ may be at home in the heart.
The first picture comes from the garden and the second from the building site. A life needs both, and for both the soil and foundation are love.
vv: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father,
Standing was a common posture for prayer in the Jewish and early Christian world. Kneeling expresses special earnestness, as it does in the Great Fast, when our Church bends the knee in prayer.
and that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, as you are being rooted and grounded in love.

The Greek speaks of a rooting already done that lasts, and the English “as you are being” brings out that it goes on. Roots grow slowly and out of sight. Simeon and Anna had been growing such roots for most of their lives.
and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge,
A deliberate paradox. We are to know what is beyond knowing. The first thing that Christian learning discovers is how much more there is.
ch: The Catechism quotes this prayer when it speaks of the Spirit strengthening the inner person so that Christ may dwell in the heart (CCC 2714). It also cites v. 14 when it says that God's fatherhood is the source of human fatherhood, and so of the honour owed to parents (CCC 2214). On this day we may apply that to the elders of our parishes.

r.h: A man and a woman who waited
set: This reading continues the scene of the Lord's Entrance and adds Anna. Luke likes to set a man and a woman side by side: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna. Two witnesses were needed for a testimony under the Law (Deuteronomy 19:15), and here the two are a devout man and a prophet who is an aged widow.

Together they stand for the people Luke calls those who were looking forward to God's coming: the “poor of the Lord”, who had nothing to rely on but his promise. The Catechism calls such people the great achievement of the Holy Spirit's hidden work in the time before Christ (CCC 716).
str: vv. 25–27: Simeon: righteous, waiting, led by the Spirit.
vv. 28–32: the child in his arms, and his song.
vv. 33–35: the blessing and the word to Mary.
vv. 36–38: Anna: her life, and what she does at that moment.
kw: The comfort promised to Israel in Isaiah 40:1: “Comfort, O comfort my people”. The title Paraclete, given to the Holy Spirit, comes from the same family of words.
Luke gives Anna a title, a father, Phanuel, and a tribe, Asher. Asher belonged to the northern tribes, and so she is a sign that God has not forgotten any part of his people.

“The redemption of Jerusalem” echoes Isaiah 52:9: “the Lord has comforted his people, he has redeemed Jerusalem”. Consolation in v. 25 and redemption in v. 38 frame the passage with the same verse of Isaiah.
vv: Guided by the Spirit, Simeon came into the temple;
The Holy Spirit is named three times in three verses (vv. 25, 26, 27). The same Spirit who came on Mary (1:35) is at work in this quiet old devotion. Simeon's part was to come when he was prompted.
then as a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple but worshiped there with fasting and prayer night and day.

The Greek could also mean that she had been a widow for eighty-four years. Either way, Luke is praising a long fidelity. Fasting and prayer are the very things our Church is about to take up in the Great Fast.
At that moment she came, and began to praise God and to speak about the child to all who were looking for the redemption of Jerusalem.
Simeon speaks to God and to Mary; Anna speaks to everybody. Luke tells us she was “of a great age” (2:36), and she goes on telling the news. Nobody is too old to proclaim the gospel.
ch: The Church reads Simeon and Anna as the Old Testament arriving at its goal: with them, all Israel comes to meet its Saviour (CCC 529). A Latin antiphon that goes back to ancient times says that the old man carried the child, but the child guided the old man (in substance). Many Christians know Simeon's song by heart as a prayer at the close of the day. The advice of 1 Timothy 5:3 that widows be honoured finds a fine image here.

qa: Was Simeon an old man, and was he a priest?

Luke says neither thing directly. He says that Simeon was promised he would not die before seeing the Messiah, and that he now asks to be dismissed (2:26, 29), so Christians have always pictured him as old. Luke does not call him a priest, though the Syriac tradition, in St Ephrem for example, does so. Our Church honours him for what the Gospel does say: he was righteous and devout, and the Holy Spirit rested on him.
rite: Mar and Morth are the Syriac titles of honour, “my lord” and “my lady”, that our Church gives to her saints. So the two from the Temple are named in our calendar as we name our own holy ones. They remind us that the saints of the Syriac calendar do not begin with the Church: the holy people of Israel come first, and we are grafted onto them.
study: Who are the Simeons and Annas of my parish, and have I ever thanked them or asked them to pray for me?
Paul prays to be “rooted and grounded in love”. What daily habit is growing roots in my life, and what is pulling them up?

lead: Paul tells the Christians of Rome that the gospel is both a debt he owes and a power he is not ashamed of. Jesus tells his hearers that the road to life is narrow. Our Church reads these on the memorial of St John de Britto, who owed the gospel to the people of the Tamil country and paid with his life.

set: Paul writes to a Church he has not founded or yet seen, probably from Corinth in the later 50s. He hopes to visit on his way to Spain (15:24, 28). These verses end his introduction and state the theme of the whole letter (vv. 16–17). Everything up to chapter 11 unfolds them.
str: v. 13: his plans to visit, so far hindered.
vv. 14–15: a debtor to all, and eager to preach in Rome too.
vv. 16–17: the theme of the letter: the gospel as God's power, God's righteousness revealed, and the quotation from Habakkuk.
kw: The word for someone who owes. He has received Christ's gift, and so he owes it to everyone else, Greeks and “barbarians”, the wise and the foolish, as he says.
The gospel is not only news about God's power. It is the power itself at work. Dynamis is also the Gospels' word for Jesus' mighty works.
Here this means God's own faithfulness in saving, and the right standing that he gives. It is the leading idea of the letter, and it is a gift received in faith.
vv: I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish
“Barbarians” meant those who did not speak Greek, with no thought of savagery. Paul's list is not a list of those who deserve the gospel. It is simply everybody.
For I am not ashamed of the gospel; it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who has faith, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

The saying echoes Jesus' warning about those who are ashamed of him (Mark 8:38). In the Rome of that day a crucified Lord was an embarrassment. “To the Jew first”: Paul never lets go of Israel's place, and God's call to her is not withdrawn (Romans 11:29; CCC 839).
“The one who is righteous will live by faith.”
Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4, where the prophet speaks of the faithfulness of the just in hard times. Faith here is both trust in God and steady fidelity to him.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the disciple must not only keep the faith but profess it and bear witness to it with confidence (CCC 1816). It also treats justification as the first work of God's grace, given through faith in Christ (CCC 1987–1992). In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a Joint Declaration on this doctrine, in which they state a shared understanding of it: by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work.

set: The Sermon on the Mount ends with choices: two gates, two kinds of fruit, two houses (7:13–27). The teaching has been given. Now the hearer must decide. The picture of two ways is old in Israel: “Choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19). The Didache, an early Church manual, opens with it: there are two ways, one of life and one of death (Didache 1).
str: v. 13: the command, and the wide gate.
v. 14: the narrow gate, the hard road, the few.
kw: Luke's version has “the narrow door” (Luke 13:24). It is small enough that one cannot pass through it with everything one is carrying.
Literally “pressed in”. It comes from the same root as thlipsis, the New Testament's usual word for affliction. The road to life passes through the pressure that disciples can expect.
vv: “Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the road is easy that leads to destruction, and there are many who take it.
Jesus does not describe a hard God. He describes an honest road. Nobody drifts through the narrow gate by accident; it has to be chosen.
For the gate is narrow and the road is hard that leads to life, and there are few who find it.
The goal is life, and this is the word to hold on to. In John, Jesus says, “I am the gate” (John 10:9). The narrow gate has a human face.
ch: The Catechism cites this saying when it speaks of the urgent call to conversion (CCC 1036), and it sets the two ways before the reader at the start of its moral teaching: the way of Christ leads to life, and a contrary way leads to destruction (CCC 1696). It is a warning, not a head count.

qa: Does “few” mean that most people will not be saved?

Jesus does not answer that question, and when he is asked directly he turns it back into a call: “Strive to enter” (Luke 13:23–24). The Church does not say how many are saved. She prays “that no one should be lost” (CCC 1058), and she teaches that God's grace can reach those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the gospel (Lumen Gentium 16). The saying is meant for me: am I on the road?
rite: St John de Britto was born in Lisbon in 1647 and became a Jesuit. He asked to go to the Madurai mission, and from the 1670s he lived among the Tamil people as a pandaram, a poor ascetic teacher, walking barefoot and eating simply. The people called him Arul Anandar. He was arrested and tortured more than once, and he was sent back to Portugal, but he returned. He was beheaded at Oriyur on 4 February 1693, and Pius XII canonized him in 1947. To this saint of our own land, a stranger who made himself a debtor, we entrust all who suffer for the name of Christ in many lands, and we pray for them and for those who have wronged them.
study: Paul counts himself a debtor to everyone. To whom do I owe the gospel, starting at home?
What in my life will not fit through a narrow gate, and what would I need to put down in this Great Fast?

lead: Two warnings for a Church about to begin its Fast. Paul reminds the Corinthians that a people can receive every gift of God and still fall, and he adds that God is faithful in every testing. Jesus tells his disciples not to be surprised if the world does not love them. Neither reading frightens for its own sake: both end with the Lord's faithfulness to his own.

set: Paul writes from Ephesus (16:8), probably about the year 54 or 55, to a Church in a great port city. In chapters 8–10 he answers a practical question: may Christians eat food offered to idols, and go to meals in temples? Some in Corinth felt that their Baptism and the Eucharist made them safe. So Paul retells the story of Israel in the desert. His own people, he says, had their “baptism” and their “spiritual food”, and yet many fell.
He calls them “our ancestors” even when writing to many who were Gentiles. Israel's story is the family story of all Christians.
str: vv. 1–4: all received the gifts: cloud, sea, food, drink, rock. The word “all” comes five times.
v. 5: but most of them fell in the wilderness.
vv. 6–10: four warnings, from Exodus and Numbers: idolatry, immorality, testing the Lord, complaining.
vv. 11–12: this was written for us; watch out.
v. 13: God's faithfulness in testing.
kw: An impression left by a seal, then a pattern. From this word comes the Christian reading of the Old Testament called typology, in which events foreshadow Christ.
Paul uses the noun and the verb for both the desert and present life. It can mean both a trial from outside and a temptation from within.
A way through, like a pass out of a narrow valley. God does not always remove the test, but he makes a path.
vv: and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.

Exodus and Numbers tell of water from a rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). Some Jewish writings of the time knew a tradition of a rock or a well that went along with Israel. Paul takes it up and says who was really giving them drink.
We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did, and were destroyed by serpents.
A note on the text. Manuscripts differ here. Some have “Christ”, as the NRSV does; others have “the Lord”, as the Malayalam POC does. The story is in Numbers 21:4–9.

No testing has overtaken you that is not common to everyone. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond your strength, but with the testing he will also provide the way out so that you may be able to endure it.
After these warnings comes this word of comfort. Our trial is not unique, and we do not face it alone. What is promised is not the absence of the trial, but the power to endure it.
ch: The Catechism draws on this chapter when it teaches the spiritual sense of Scripture: the crossing of the Red Sea is a sign of Christ's victory and of Christian Baptism (CCC 117; see also 128–129). It also teaches: “What God commands he makes possible by his grace” (CCC 2082). St Augustine says God does not command the impossible, but in commanding he tells you to do what you can, and to ask for what you cannot (in substance), words which the Council of Trent took up.

set: We are at the table on the night before the Passion. Jesus has just said, “love one another” (15:17), and now he speaks of what love will meet outside. In John, “the world” (kosmos) can mean what God so loves (3:16). Here it means human life when it is closed against God.

A word on “they”, and on “their law” in v. 25. Jesus and his first disciples were Jews, and these words are not about the Jewish people. Many scholars think that John's wording also reflects painful later disputes between his community and synagogue leaders. The Church teaches that the Jews are not to be held responsible, as a people, for the death of Jesus (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). This passage speaks of anyone, in any time, who shuts out the light.
str: vv. 18–19: the world's hatred, and the reason for it: you were chosen out of it.
vv. 20–21: the servant shares the master's lot.
vv. 22–24: having seen and heard, they have no excuse.
v. 25: the Scripture is fulfilled.
kw: One of John's great words. God loves the world and sends his Son to save it (3:16–17); here it is the world as a system closed to God. So a disciple is sent into the world, and does not belong to it (17:14–18).
The word comes seven times in these eight verses. Jesus says it plainly, so that it will not take his disciples by surprise (16:1, 4).
“For nothing”, the same word used elsewhere for a gift given without charge. It is the sad twin of grace. Grace loves us for nothing; here people hate him for nothing.
vv: “If the world hates you, be aware that it hated me before it hated you.
This is a comfort, not a threat. The disciple who is opposed is standing where the Lord stood.
If they persecuted me, they will persecute you; if they kept my word, they will keep yours also.
Both halves count. Some will reject the witness, and some will receive it. The apostle's word has the same fate as his Master's.
It was to fulfill the word that is written in their law, ‘They hated me without a cause.’
The phrase comes from the Psalms (35:19; 69:4). “Law” here means Scripture as a whole. Psalm 69 is one of the Psalms the New Testament most often applies to the Passion.
ch: The Second Vatican Council says that some Christians have been called, and will always be called, to give the supreme witness of love before all people and especially before persecutors (Lumen Gentium 42). St Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to die in Rome, wrote that Christianity shows its greatness most when it is hated by the world (in substance; Letter to the Romans 3). In our day, too, we remember all who suffer for Christ in many lands, and we pray for them and for those who have wronged them.

qa: Paul says twenty-three thousand fell. Numbers says twenty-four thousand. Why the difference?

Paul seems to be recalling Numbers 25:9, which has “twenty-four thousand”. Interpreters offer several explanations: a slip of memory in dictation, a round figure, or a blend with another verse. The Church's teaching on the truth of Scripture does not depend on such figures. It looks at what God wished to teach for our salvation (Dei Verbum 11). Paul's point is not arithmetic, but that privilege does not protect from sin.
study: “If you think you are standing, watch out that you do not fall.” Where do I feel most safe from sin, and might that be the very place to watch?
Have I ever been laughed at or left out because of my faith? How does John 15:18 change the way I carry that?

lead: On the eve of Kothine Sunday, when the Great Fast opens, both readings talk about money. First Timothy tells the rich where to set their hope. Jesus tells of a rich man who spoke only to himself and heard God's voice too late. The question for the Fast is plain: what is my wealth for?

r.h: The life that really is life
set: The letter is addressed to Timothy, left in charge of the Church at Ephesus (1:3), a rich city. It names Paul as its author, though many scholars think the Pastoral Letters come from a later disciple writing in his name, while others defend Paul's authorship; the Church receives them as inspired Scripture either way.

Earlier in the chapter comes the warning that “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil” (6:10). These last verses show that there were rich members in the community, and that the writer does not tell them to leave. He tells them how to be rich as Christians.
str: v. 17: what the rich are not to do: be haughty, or hope in riches.
v. 18: what they are to do: good works and sharing.
v. 19: the true investment.
vv. 20–21: a last charge to Timothy: guard what has been entrusted.
kw: Literally to think high. The first danger of wealth, the writer says, is what it does to one's view of oneself.
From the word koinōnia, communion. It is the same family of words that describes the common life of the first Church (Acts 2:42). Sharing money is a form of communion.
A deposit left with someone for safe keeping, to be returned whole. The Catechism takes this word into its teaching on the “sacred deposit” of the faith (CCC 84).
vv: As for those who in the present age are rich, command them not to be haughty, or to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but rather on God who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment.
This is not hostility to the good things of creation: God gives them “for our enjoyment”. The contrast is between two places to put one's hope, and one of them is unsure.
They are to do good, to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share,
A play on words: be rich, in a different currency. The true measure of riches is what passes through the hands.
Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid the profane chatter and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge;
“Knowledge” here is gnōsis. St Irenaeus took the phrase “falsely called knowledge” into the title of his great work against the Gnostics around the year 180.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the goods of creation are destined for the whole human race (CCC 2402), and that the tenth commandment forbids greed (CCC 2536). It quotes St John Chrysostom: “Not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life. The goods we possess are not ours, but theirs” (CCC 2446).

set: A man in the crowd has just asked Jesus to make his brother divide the family inheritance (12:13). Jesus refuses to act as judge, warns against “all kinds of greed”, and adds that “one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions” (12:15). This parable, found only in Luke, is his illustration. Right after it comes the teaching about the ravens and the lilies (12:22–31).
str: v. 16: a good harvest, which in itself is a blessing.
vv. 17–19: the rich man's talk with himself.
v. 20: God's word.
v. 21: the lesson.
kw: The word of the Psalms: “Fools say in their hearts, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1). The man is not a thief. His folly is that he lives as if God were not there.
The man speaks to his “soul” about the long years ahead (v. 19), and in v. 20 God tells him that this same psychē is being demanded. The Malayalam POC keeps “ആത്മാവ്” in both places.
Being rich “toward God”. Riches have a direction. In the verses that follow, Jesus will say: “Sell your possessions, and give alms” (12:33).
vv: And he thought to himself, ‘What should I do, for I have no place to store my crops?’

He is the only one in his own story. Nobody else, not a family member, not a neighbour, not a poor person, appears in the whole of his thinking. St Basil, preaching on this passage, gives the answer he should have found: the bread you store up belongs to the hungry (in substance).
And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’
Enjoying life is not the sin. The sin is the plan, in which his soul's whole future is built on barns.
But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life is being demanded of you. And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’

This is the only voice in the story apart from his own. “Demanded” is the language of a loan called in. Life itself was only ever on loan, and the question at the end brings us back to the brothers and their inheritance.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything, and it warns against attachment to riches (CCC 2544–2547). St Ambrose, writing on the rich man's barns in his book on Naboth, says that the bosoms of the poor, the homes of widows and the mouths of children are the barns that last for ever (in substance). In the Great Fast now at the door, almsgiving is not an extra, but one of the three pillars of Christian penance, together with fasting and prayer (CCC 1434).

qa: Is it wrong to save money or to be rich?

The reading does not say so. The man's harvest is good, and the Bible praises foresight (Proverbs 6:6–8). First Timothy addresses the rich without telling them to leave. The Church recognises the right to private property, while teaching that created goods are meant for all (CCC 2402–2403). The fault in the parable is that he saved for himself alone and left God out. The question for me is whether there are others, and God, in my plans for what I own.
study: If I had an unexpected surplus this month, who would be in my thinking besides myself?
What practical alms will my family decide on for the coming Great Fast, and how much will it actually cost us?

lead: Our Church opens the Great Fast at a wedding. On Kothine Sunday, the Sunday of Cana, the first thing we are shown is not ashes but wine. The season that follows is meant to change us, as water was changed, and today's readings teach how.

The lectionary is full. The Evening Gospel has the Good Shepherd in the Temple at the feast of Dedication: “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:27). The Old Testament lessons give the covenant sign after the flood, “I have set my bow in the clouds” (Genesis 9:13), the commandments at Sinai (Exodus 20:7–22), and Joel's call, “rend your hearts and not your clothing” (Joel 2:13). In Acts we meet the Church of Antioch, “and it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called ‘Christians’” (Acts 11:26). That city is the mother of our own Antiochene tradition.

Three readings are studied here. In Isaiah, God tells a disappointed people what kind of fast he wants. In Colossians, Paul describes the change of clothes that begins at Baptism. In John, Jesus turns water for purification into the wine of a wedding. The key words of this Sunday are fast, clothing and sign.

set: Of the Old Testament lessons this one speaks most directly to the season, and like Cana it ends in delight. Many scholars think that the last chapters of Isaiah (56–66) address the community after the return from exile in Babylon, about the late sixth century BC. Life was hard, the rebuilding was slow, and the great promises seemed unfulfilled.

Just before our reading the people complain: “Why do we fast, but you do not see?” (58:3). God's reply is sharp: on your fast day you serve your own interest and oppress your workers (58:3–4). Today's passage is the second half of that answer. The prophet does not attack fasting. He tells them what fasting is for.
str: vv. 6–7: the true fast: justice and bread.
vv. 8–9a: the promise: light, healing, and an answer: “Here I am”.
vv. 9b–12: the same call and promise again, with the picture of the watered garden and the rebuilt city.
vv. 13–14: the sabbath: a day of delight in the Lord.
kw: A fast in Israel was going without food as a sign of grief or of humility before God. God does not take away the word; he widens it.
The Hebrew of v. 7 is literally “to break your bread for the hungry”. It is the ordinary verb for breaking a loaf. Christians can hardly hear it without thinking of the altar.
“If you call the sabbath a delight” (v. 13), then “you shall take delight in the Lord” (v. 14). A chapter on fasting ends with joy, as the Fast itself will.
vv: Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice, to undo the thongs of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?
Four verbs of releasing. It is a fast from holding others down. Luke shows Jesus reading Isaiah at Nazareth, and a phrase from this very verse is woven into the text he reads (Luke 4:18).
Is it not to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; when you see the naked, to cover them, and not to hide yourself from your own kin?
The list comes very close to the judgment scene in Matthew 25:35–36. The last clause reaches home: the poor include relatives we would prefer not to see.
Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry for help, and he will say, Here I am.
In verse 3 the people were complaining that God did not see them. The answer is here. When the people turn to the needy, God says the words that a servant says to his master: Here I am.
if you offer your food to the hungry and satisfy the needs of the afflicted, then your light shall rise in the darkness and your gloom be like the noonday.
Light comes as we give, not after we have sorted ourselves out. What we go looking for in the Fast often arrives while we are serving someone else.
ch: The Catechism teaches that penance is first of all conversion of the heart, without which fasting and mortification remain empty (CCC 1430), and that it is expressed above all in fasting, prayer and almsgiving (CCC 1434). Its list of the corporal works of mercy, feeding the hungry, sheltering the homeless, clothing the naked, could have come from this page (CCC 2447). St John Chrysostom, preaching in Antioch during the Fast of the year 387, tells his hearers to show that they are fasting by their works: pity the poor man and be reconciled with your enemy (in substance; Homilies on the Statues 3). St Leo the Great says in his Lenten sermons that what we deny ourselves should become food for the poor (in substance).

set: The letter names Paul as its author, though many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way. The letter's first half shows who Christ is, and then, from 3:1, how those who “have been raised with Christ” ought to live. These lines read like instruction to the newly baptized.

Some in Colossae seem to have been attracted to rules about food and festivals, and to severe practices that promised to control the body (2:16–23). Paul says that such practices have no real power (2:23). The change comes from a death and a new life in Christ. This is a useful warning at the start of a Fast.
str: vv. 5–7: put to death: a list of five vices, and the note that this was once your life.
vv. 8–11: put away: a second list of five; the old self is off, the new is on, and the old divisions fall.
vv. 12–14: clothe yourselves: a list of five virtues, then forgiveness and love over everything.
vv. 15–17: the peace, the word, the song, and thanks in all that you do.
kw: A strong word: do not merely trim, but kill. Paul has already said “you have died” (3:3). We are to become what we already are by Baptism.
Literally “wanting more”. Paul calls it idolatry, since what we endlessly want becomes our god.

The language of dressing, used with “stripped off” in vv. 9–10. It is one of the New Testament's pictures of Baptism: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27).
From the word for the umpire at the games, found only here in the New Testament. When things are disputed in the heart, Christ's peace gets to make the call.
vv: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have stripped off the old self with its practices

Paul's reason for the moral command is sacramental. Your Baptism already took off that garment. St Cyril of Jerusalem told the newly baptized that taking off their tunic before the font was an image of putting off the old self (in substance).
In that renewal there is no longer Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave and free; but Christ is all and in all!
The Scythians were regarded in that world as the wildest of all. Every wall that the old life thought normal is named here and is taken down.
just as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive.
This is the measure of forgiveness. It is exactly what our Church puts before us at the Shubkono on the Monday after this Sunday, when we ask each other's pardon before going on.
Above all, clothe yourselves with love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
Love is the outer garment and belt that holds all the rest in place. The Malayalam POC says “practise” (പരിശീലിക്കുവിൻ), and that is true as well: love is a skill to be learned by doing.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly;
“Dwell” is the same family of words as “house”. Scripture is to be at home among us, and here it is sung as well as read. Our Syriac tradition has always taught its faith through hymns.
ch: The Catechism says that charity is the bond of all the virtues, and quotes v. 14 (CCC 1827). The white garment given at Baptism symbolizes that the baptized person has put on Christ (CCC 1243). On the Church's song, it teaches that singing is bound up with the liturgy (CCC 1156–1158), and it recalls the apostle's words on psalms, hymns and spiritual songs (CCC 2641). The tenth commandment's warning about greed takes up Paul's concern (CCC 2536).

r.h: You have kept the good wine until now
set: John calls this the first of Jesus' “signs”. It comes after the calling of the first disciples (1:35–51). “On the third day” may simply count from the last scene, and readers have also heard in it a first hint of the third day of the Resurrection. A village wedding in Galilee could last for days, and the wine was the family's honour. To run out would have brought real shame on the hosts.

John never gives the mother of Jesus her name. She appears twice in this Gospel, at Cana and at the Cross (19:25–27), and both times Jesus calls her “Woman”. The first sign and the final hour are joined by her presence.
str: vv. 1–2: the wedding and the guests.
vv. 3–5: the mother's words, the Son's answer, and her word to the servants.
vv. 6–8: six stone jars, filled and drawn from.
vv. 9–10: the steward tastes, and calls the bridegroom.
v. 11: John's comment: sign, glory, faith.
kw: John does not use the usual word for a miracle, “mighty work”. A sign points beyond itself. The point of Cana is not the wine, but the one who gives it.
“My hour has not yet come” (v. 4). In John, the hour is the Passion and glorification (12:23; 13:1). Already at a wedding feast the Cross is on his mind.

A respectful form of address in Greek, though unusual from a son to his mother. It may recall the woman of Genesis 3:15, and it is the same word he uses from the Cross (19:26). See the question below.
vv: When the wine gave out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”
She does not command, nor does she even ask. She simply lays the need before him. This is one of the best lessons in prayer in the Gospels.
His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”
These are the last words of Mary recorded in John. They recall Pharaoh's words about Joseph in the famine: “what he says to you, do” (Genesis 41:55). All Marian devotion is meant to lead here.
Now standing there were six stone water jars for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.

Stone jars were favoured for purification water, because Jewish law held that stone did not take on impurity. By the NRSV's figures this is at least a hundred and twenty gallons. It is far more than any wedding needs, and overflowing abundance is one of the marks of God's new age (Amos 9:13; Joel 3:18).
Jesus said to them, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them up to the brim.

The servants do the ordinary work, and they carry water without knowing what is coming. Jesus makes use of what we bring, and it is always water. In the Fast, too, our part is to fill the jars to the brim.
But you have kept the good wine until now.”
The steward does not know how true his words are. God has kept the best for the last, in his Son. These words may also be heard from Qyomtho looking back on the Fast.
and his disciples believed in him.
The purpose of the sign. At the Cross this faith will be tested, and the mother who is here will still be there.
ch: The Church sees in Cana Christ's confirmation of the goodness of marriage (CCC 1613). She also reads in it the Eucharist: the miracle announces the hour of Jesus' glorification and the new wine that has become his Blood (CCC 1335). The Catechism says that at Cana the mother asks her Son for the needs of a wedding feast, and that this is the sign of another feast, the wedding of the Lamb (CCC 2618). St Cyril of Jerusalem argues to the newly baptized that he who once changed water into wine can surely change wine into his Blood (in substance). St Augustine remarks that the Lord who made wine in these jars does the same every year in the vines, and we have stopped being amazed (in substance). St Ephrem, in a hymn on Cana, invites the Lord to a wedding feast of song, and asks him to fill his mouth with praise as he filled those jars (in substance; Hymns on Virginity 33).

qa: Why does the Great Fast begin with a wedding?

Because the Fast is a road to a feast, and the Church wants us to know where we are going. Jesus himself calls his presence a wedding (Mark 2:19–20). Beginning at Cana teaches that the aim of penance is not gloom but change. It is the water that is changed, and we are the water.
Was Jesus being rude to his mother?

No. “Woman” was a respectful way to speak, and he uses it again from the Cross, as he entrusts her to the beloved disciple. The Greek phrase in v. 4, which the POC translates literally (എനിക്കും നിനക്കും എന്ത്?), can sound like distance. But the phrase is an idiom whose force depends on the tone and setting, and Mary plainly did not hear it as a refusal: she turns straight to the servants. Jesus acts on her word, and the Church has always found in this the power of her intercession (CCC 2618).
Does changing the water for purification mean that Jewish worship was worthless?

No. John shows that what God gave to Israel comes to fullness in Jesus, and that fullness is a gift, not a verdict. The Church says that God's gifts and calling to the Jewish people are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; CCC 839), and that Christians share a great spiritual patrimony with them (Nostra Aetate 4). Jesus and the disciples at the table, and the mother who noticed the wine, were Jews at a Jewish wedding.
rite: Kothine opens the Sundays of the Great Fast in our Malankara tradition. The Sundays ahead read the Lord's healings: Garbo next week is the healing of the leper, and M'shario after it the healing of the paralytic. So the season moves from the wine of Cana to the bodies and souls that Christ restores, and it goes on to Holy Week and Qyomtho. On the Monday after Kothine comes the Shubkono, the service of forgiveness, when we ask pardon of one another. Colossians 3:13 could stand over the church door that day. Every Holy Qurbono of the Fast is a small Cana: at the altar wine becomes his Blood, and we are asked once more to do whatever he tells us.
study: Isaiah 58:6–7 lists what God wants from a fast. If I chose one line of it for this Fast, which would it be, and what would I actually do?
Paul speaks of taking off and putting on. What one habit will I take off in the next seven weeks, and what one will I put on?
Mary says, “They have no wine.” What need in my family or parish should I simply lay before Jesus today?
What is the plain water in my life that I can fill up to the brim, trusting him for the rest?

lead: The Great Fast begins with a lesson in how to begin. Shubkono, the service of forgiveness, is its door, and the epistle (Ephesians 4:25–32) gives it words: “forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you” (4:32). Genesis gives the root: Abram, with nothing to show for God's promise, believes the God who made it. The Gospel gives the pattern: Jesus, forty days in the wilderness, answers the tempter from the word of God. Peace with one another, trust in God, and the word as our food: that is the Fast.

set: Genesis 12–25 tell the story of Abraham, who is still called Abram here. God has promised him land, descendants and blessing (12:1–3), and no child has come. “After these things” points back to chapter 14, where Abram went to war to rescue Lot. God's first word, “Do not be afraid”, suggests what is in his heart. This is the first time in Genesis that Abram's own words to God are recorded, and they are a complaint.
str: v. 1: the word of the Lord comes in a vision.
vv. 2–3: Abram's complaint: no child, and a servant as his heir.
vv. 4–5: the promise: a son of his own, and descendants like the stars.
v. 6: Abram believes, and the Lord reckons it to him as righteousness.
kw: The soldier's hand shield. God does not promise Abram a shield; he says that he himself is one. The Psalms take up the same word many times.
From the root ’āman, to be firm or solid. The word Amen comes from the same root. To believe is to rest one's whole weight on God as on firm ground.
A word for counting and crediting. Abram's trust is entered to his account as righteousness. Paul builds on this verse in Romans 4 and Galatians 3.
vv: Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.
God speaks first. The promise comes before Abram has asked for anything.
Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.
Abram has been looking at what he lacks. God takes him outside and makes him look up. The answer to his complaint is not an explanation but a wider sky.
And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.
Nothing has changed yet: there is still no child. Abram's only act is to trust. This short verse becomes one of the most quoted in the whole New Testament teaching on faith.
ch: The Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith, and uses this verse in the form Paul quotes it: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (CCC 144–146). St Paul makes it the ground of his teaching in Romans 4 and Galatians 3, and St James reads it together with Abraham's obedience (James 2:21–23). At the opening of the Fast it tells us where our discipline must begin: not with what we can show God, but with what God has promised.

r.h: Forty days and the word of God
set: Matthew places this scene straight after the baptism of Jesus, where the voice from heaven says, “This is my Son, the Beloved” (3:17). The tempter now begins twice with “If you are the Son of God”. The Spirit who came down at the Jordan leads Jesus into the wilderness. Israel was tested in the wilderness for forty years (Deuteronomy 8:2). Jesus, the Son, walks that road in forty days and stays faithful. All three of his answers come from Deuteronomy.
str: vv. 1–2: led by the Spirit; the forty days of fasting.
vv. 3–4: the first test: stones into bread.
vv. 5–7: the second test: the pinnacle of the temple.
vv. 8–10: the third test: all the kingdoms of the world.
v. 11: the devil leaves, and angels wait on him.
kw: One Greek word covers both meanings. The Spirit leads Jesus to the place of testing; the devil tries to turn the testing into a fall.
Diabolos means slanderer or accuser, and Satan comes from the Hebrew word for adversary. The story uses both (4:1, 4:10).

The tense means that it stands written and still holds. Jesus uses no display of power, only the word. The devil quotes Scripture too (Psalm 91:11–12), which shows that even the word can be twisted when it is torn from its sense.
vv: He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterwards he was famished.
Moses (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8) also went forty days. The hunger is real: the Son is truly human, and the test comes at his weakest point.
One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
From Deuteronomy 8:3, where Moses explains the manna. Jesus does not despise bread; he will feed crowds. He refuses to use his Sonship for himself.
Away with you, Satan! for it is written, ‘Worship the Lord your God, and serve only him.’

From Deuteronomy 6:13. The offer of all the kingdoms is a road to power without the Cross. Jesus refuses it, and at the end of the Gospel the Risen Lord says that all authority has been given to him (28:18).
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus is the new Adam, who stayed faithful where the first Adam gave in, and that he fulfils Israel's vocation perfectly (CCC 539). It adds, in the Latin Church's own wording: “By the solemn forty days of Lent the Church unites herself each year to the mystery of Jesus in the desert” (CCC 540). St John Chrysostom says that the Lord went into temptation straight after baptism so that the baptized would not be thrown into confusion when trials come (in substance, Homilies on Matthew 13). St Augustine says that in Christ we ourselves were tempted, and in him we overcome (in substance, on Psalm 60).

qa: Why does the Spirit lead Jesus to be tempted, if God tempts no one?

God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13). The Spirit leads Jesus into the place of testing, as God led Israel in the wilderness, and the evil comes from the tempter. Jesus enters our condition so that he can help us: “Because he himself was tested by what he suffered, he is able to help those who are being tested” (Hebrews 2:18).
rite: Shubkono comes from the Syriac word for forgiveness. Our Church does not start the Fast by counting foods. The priest bows before the people and asks their pardon, and the faithful ask pardon of one another. It stands beside today's epistle as its living form: “do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). With that peace we can walk the road of the Fast together.
study: Abram believed when nothing had yet changed. Which promise of God am I finding hard to trust in this Great Fast?
Jesus answered each test from Scripture. Which word of God will I carry with me through this Fast? Whom do I need to forgive before I begin?

lead: Abram has believed; now he asks how he can know. God answers with a rite and with a hard word: his descendants will suffer before they are delivered. The epistle (Romans 8:1–11) speaks to people who still struggle in the flesh: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (8:1). In the Gospel the God who made promises to Abram comes in person as the shepherd who lays down his life. Faith does not remove the dark. It knows who is with us in it.

set: The scene continues the same chapter. Abram has believed the promise of a son (15:6), and God now turns to the promise of land. The animals he is told to bring belong to a covenant rite. In the ancient Near East those making a solemn pact could cut animals in two and pass between the parts; Jeremiah 34:18 is the clearest witness in the Bible. The passing itself comes in vv. 17–21. Here the pieces are laid out and Abram waits.
str: v. 7: God names himself as the one who brought Abram from Ur.
v. 8: Abram's question.
vv. 9–11: the animals are cut in two, and Abram drives away the birds of prey.
v. 12: deep sleep and terrifying darkness.
vv. 13–16: God foretells slavery in a foreign land, judgment on the oppressor, and the return.
kw: The same word as the sleep God sent on Adam (Genesis 2:21). It is more than tiredness: a sleep that God sends when he is about to do something the person cannot do or watch for himself.

A foreigner living in a land not his own, without the rights of its people. Abraham's descendants will be strangers, and the Law later tells Israel to care for the stranger because of this memory (Exodus 22:21).
From the verb ‘ānāh, to afflict or humble. The same verb describes what Egypt did to Israel in Exodus 1:11–12. God sees that history before it begins.
vv: O Lord God, how am I to know that I shall possess it?
This comes just after “he believed”. Faith is not silence. A believer may ask God how, and God does not rebuke Abram; he answers.
And when birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away.
A small, plain act. All Abram can do is keep watch over what he has laid before God until God acts. It is a good picture of the patient side of a fast.
your offspring shall be aliens in a land that is not theirs, and shall be slaves there, and they shall be oppressed for four hundred years

God does not hide the long dark from Abram. The number is a round one: Exodus 12:40 gives 430 years. Verse 16 adds that the land is given in God's own time and with his justice: “the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete”.
ch: St Stephen recalls this promise in his speech (Acts 7:6–7), and the Letter to the Hebrews sees Abraham as a pilgrim who “set out, not knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8). The Catechism teaches that God in his providence can draw good even from the consequences of evil, though we often see it only with time (CCC 312). The Church reads this passage as a school of hope: God's promise stands even when the road to it passes through suffering.

set: John 10 follows the healing of the man born blind (John 9), and it is addressed to those who should have cared for him. The picture has deep roots. In Ezekiel 34 God speaks against shepherds who feed themselves and then says, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (34:15). When Jesus says “I am the good shepherd”, he stands where Psalm 23 and Ezekiel place God himself.
str: v. 11: the shepherd lays down his life.
vv. 12–13: the hired hand runs away.
vv. 14–15: mutual knowledge, like that of the Father and the Son.
v. 16: other sheep, one flock, one shepherd.
kw: More than morally good: fine, noble, true to what a shepherd should be. This is the shepherd as he was always meant to be.
A man working for wages. He is not called wicked; he simply does not own the sheep, and so when danger comes he has no reason to stay.
John alone uses this phrase in the Gospels, and repeats it (10:15, 17–18; 13:37; 15:13). Jesus' death is not something that happens to him against his will; he gives his life.
vv: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
In ordinary life a shepherd risks himself but hopes to live, since a dead shepherd leaves the flock unprotected. Here the shepherd's death is the life of the sheep.
I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father.
To know here means a bond of love, not information. The disciple is drawn into the very relationship of the Son and the Father.
So there will be one flock, one shepherd.
The “other sheep” are commonly understood as the Gentiles who would come to believe (compare John 11:52). The unity comes from the one voice they hear.
ch: The Catechism, following Vatican II, calls the Church a flock of which God foretold that he would be the shepherd (CCC 754; Lumen Gentium 6). It also says that Christ always gives his Church the gift of unity, and that she must always pray and work to preserve and perfect it (CCC 820). St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, asks his people whether they know the shepherd not only by faith but by love and by what they do (in substance, Homilies on the Gospels 14).

study: Abram asks God, “how am I to know?” What honest question do I need to bring to God in prayer this week?
The hired hand leaves because the sheep are not his own. Who has been given to my care, and where am I tempted to run away?

lead: The covenant with Abram is sealed in the dark, and only God passes between the pieces. The promise rests on his faithfulness. Paul, who knew that faithfulness, still says: “I press on toward the goal for the prize of the heavenly call of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:14). In the Gospel Jesus asks the question each disciple must answer, and Peter replies. On the day our Church gives thanks for its rank as a Major Archiepiscopal Church, these readings set both the gift and the task before us.

r.h: The fire passes between the pieces
set: This closes the scene that began at 15:7. Abram asked how he could know, the animals were cut in two, and he fell into a deep sleep. Jeremiah 34:18 shows what passing between the parts meant: those who walked between them called on themselves the fate of the slain animal if they broke their word. Now comes the surprise. Abram does not walk. Only the fire passes, and fire and smoke will later mark God's presence at the Exodus and at Sinai (Exodus 13:21; 19:18).
str: v. 17: at nightfall the fire pot and the torch pass between the pieces.
v. 18: “On that day” the Lord makes the covenant and states the gift.
vv. 19–21: a list of ten peoples of the land.
kw: A tannûr is a clay oven or fire pot. The POC has തീച്ചൂള. Smoke and flame are all that this passage shows of God.
The same word lappîd appears in the plural at Sinai for the flashes seen by the people (Exodus 20:18).
The Hebrew idiom is literally “to cut a covenant”, which is why the cutting of the animals belongs to the story.
vv: When the sun had gone down and it was dark, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.
Many commentators see here the heart of the chapter: God binds himself alone. Abram contributes nothing except the waiting.
On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram
The word “covenant” joins the promise of land to the God who has just passed between the pieces in the fire. Abram is still childless and still owns none of this land. All of it is given by word.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews draws on this kind of oath: “When God made a promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself” (Hebrews 6:13). St Paul says that the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and the Church honours the covenant with Israel, which God has not revoked (CCC 839; Nostra Aetate 4). For Christians the line runs on to the Upper Room: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). What God took on himself in figure in the dark of Genesis, Christ fulfils on the Cross, and we receive at every Holy Qurbono.

r.h: But who do you say that I am?
set: Herod has just asked, “who is this about whom I hear such things?” (9:9), and Jesus has fed the five thousand (9:10–17). Now comes the answer. Luke tells this more briefly than Mark (8:27–30) and Matthew (16:13–20). He does not name Caesarea Philippi, but he alone says that Jesus was praying. The next verses, beyond today's reading, bring the first prediction of the Passion (9:21–22), so the title must be understood through the Cross.
str: v. 18: Jesus at prayer; the question about the crowds.
v. 19: their answers: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the ancient prophets.
v. 20: the question to the disciples; Peter's confession.
kw: Luke often shows Jesus at prayer at the great turning points: the baptism (3:21), the choosing of the Twelve (6:12), the Transfiguration (9:28–29). Peter's confession comes out of that prayer.
The Greek places “you” first for emphasis. Others' opinions are heard, and then each disciple is asked directly.
Christos is the Greek for the Hebrew māšîaḥ, the anointed one. “Of God” says who anointed him and to whom he belongs.
vv: Who do the crowds say that I am?
The crowds are not hostile. They place Jesus among the great figures of the past. That is respectful, and it is not enough.
But who do you say that I am?
This question cannot be answered by reporting what others say. It is put to every generation.
The Messiah of God.
Peter speaks for the Twelve and says the true thing, though he does not yet know the road it will take.
ch: The Catechism says: “On the rock of this faith confessed by St. Peter, Christ built his Church” (CCC 424), and teaches that Peter holds the first place in the college of the Twelve because of the confession the Father revealed to him (CCC 552). What Peter says in the name of all, each Christian says personally in baptism and in the Creed.

rite: On 10 February 2005 Pope John Paul II raised the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church to the rank of a Major Archiepiscopal Church, with Moran Mor Cyril Baselios as the first Major Archbishop. This Church grew from the reunion led by Mar Ivanios in 1930. It keeps its own West Syriac, Antiochene liturgy and lives in full communion with the Bishop of Rome. Today's Gospel fits the day: the confession of Peter is the faith we share with the whole Church, and we say it in our own tradition's voice. Let us give thanks, and pray with respect and love for all our sister Churches of the Malankara tradition.
study: God bound himself alone while Abram slept. Where do I still act as if God's faithfulness depended on my own?
If Jesus asked me today, “who do you say that I am?”, what would I answer in my own words? How does my life answer it?

lead: Two women who waited on God stand side by side today. Sarai, worn down by waiting, makes a plan of her own, and three people are hurt by it. Mary, who waits and lets God act, sings. Between them the epistle gives the secret of such waiting: “your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3). On the memorial of Our Lady of Lourdes, her song turns our eyes to the lowly and the sick.

set: Ten years have passed in Canaan (16:3), and God's promise of a son to Abram (15:4) has not yet come true. Ancient Near Eastern law collections and contracts know the custom by which a childless wife gave her slave woman to her husband, and the child counted as the wife's. Sarai is doing something her world would have called sensible. The story shows what it costs. Hagar is an Egyptian and a slave, and nobody asks her anything: she is not given one word until the angel finds her in the wilderness.
str: vv. 1–2: Sarai's plan, and Abram listens.
vv. 3–4: Hagar is given to Abram; she conceives and despises her mistress.
v. 5: Sarai blames Abram.
v. 6: Abram hands Hagar over; Sarai deals harshly with her; Hagar runs away.
kw: A female slave attached to her mistress. The word is repeated through the chapter, and only the angel will call Hagar by her name.
Sarai's word in v. 5, the same word used for the violence that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11). She feels this deeply, and yet she goes on to do harm herself.

From ‘ānāh, to afflict, the same verb used of what Egypt will do to Abram's descendants (15:13; Exodus 1:11–12). Here an Egyptian slave suffers it from a Hebrew mistress. Scripture does not hide the sins of its own heroes.
vv: You see that the Lord has prevented me from bearing children
Sarai sees God's hand only as a closed door. So she tries another door. The whole chapter asks what happens when we stop waiting for God and do his work for him.
And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.

Many readers hear an echo of Eden: “you have listened to the voice of your wife” (3:17). In v. 3 she “took” and “gave” to her husband, as in 3:6. The pattern of the first sin returns inside the family of promise.
Your slave-girl is in your power; do to her as you please.
Abram, who believed so greatly in chapter 15, here does nothing to protect the woman who bears his child. The great man of faith is shown failing.
ch: The Catechism says that couples who find they cannot have children suffer greatly (CCC 2374), and it teaches that using a third person to bear a child offends against the unity of marriage (CCC 2376). It also explains that the understanding of marriage's unity developed slowly under the old Law, and that the patriarchs' polygamy was not yet explicitly rejected (CCC 1610). Scripture reports these things without approving them, and it lets us see the sorrow they bring.

set: Mary has gone in haste to Elizabeth, who has called her blessed “who believed” (1:45). This is her answer, the song known by its first Latin word, Magnificat. It is woven from the Old Testament, above all the song of Hannah, another woman God lifted up: “He raises up the poor from the dust” (1 Samuel 2:8). Mary stands as the daughter of Israel in whom the promise to Abraham reaches its goal, and the song ends with his name.
str: vv. 46–49: what God has done for Mary.
v. 50: his mercy from generation to generation.
vv. 51–53: the great reversal: the proud and the lowly, the rich and the hungry.
vv. 54–55: the promise to Abraham kept.
kw: To make great, to declare great. Mary adds nothing to God; she lets his greatness be seen. Her whole self, “my soul” and “my spirit”, does this.
Not the inner virtue only, but a low condition: being small, of no account. Hannah asks God to look on her “misery” (1 Samuel 1:11), and the Greek Bible uses this same word there.
Often taken as the Greek for the Hebrew ḥesed, God's faithful covenant love. It appears twice in the song (vv. 50, 54).
vv: for he has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant. Surely, from now on all generations will call me blessed
A village girl from Nazareth says that every age will call her blessed, and every age has. The reason is in the first half of the verse: God looked at her.
He has brought down the powerful from their thrones, and lifted up the lowly

The verbs are in the past tense, although Mary sings before any of this is visible. She speaks as the prophets do, seeing God's future as already done. Mary's joy is not a retreat from the world's suffering.
according to the promise he made to our ancestors, to Abraham and to his descendants forever
The promise of the stars in Genesis 15 is remembered here. God has not forgotten it. What Sarai could not bring about by her plan, God brings about in his own way.
