ch: The Catechism calls the Magnificat the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church, a song of thanksgiving for the fullness of graces poured out in the economy of salvation (CCC 2619). It quotes “all generations will call me blessed” as the ground of the Church's devotion to Mary (CCC 971). St Ambrose wrote: let the soul of Mary be in each of us to magnify the Lord, and the spirit of Mary to rejoice in God (in substance, on Luke).

rite: On 11 February 1858, at the grotto of Massabielle near Lourdes, the Blessed Virgin appeared to Bernadette Soubirous, a poor girl of fourteen, the first of eighteen apparitions. On 25 March she named herself: “I am the Immaculate Conception.” St John Paul II made this day the World Day of the Sick. The Magnificat fits it exactly: the Lord chose a lowly child as his witness, and the sick, who are often pushed to the edge, are given the first place. In this first week of the Great Fast, let us remember the sick of our own parish and visit one of them.
study: Sarai could not wait and made a plan of her own. Where am I doing God's work for him, and who is paying for it?
Mary sings before anything is visible. What has God already done in my life that I can thank him for today, even if much is still unfinished?

lead: A runaway slave woman in the desert gives God a name: the God who sees. Nobody in Abram's house saw her; God did. The epistle (Romans 2:12–16) widens the view: God sees also into the hearts of those who never received the Law, for “what the law requires is written on their hearts” (2:15). In the Gospel Jesus promises that he will acknowledge before the angels those who acknowledge him before others. To live this Fast is to live under the eyes of a God who sees and hears.

set: Hagar has run from Sarai's harsh treatment (16:6) and is on the way to Shur, the road toward her own country, Egypt. She is pregnant, alone and without a protector. The first time the angel of the Lord appears in the Bible, he comes to her: not to a patriarch or a king, but to a foreign slave in the wilderness.
str: vv. 7–8: the angel finds her and asks two questions.
vv. 9–10: the command to return, and a promise of countless descendants.
vv. 11–12: the announcement of the birth of Ishmael.
vv. 13–14: Hagar names God, and the well receives its name.
vv. 15–16: Ishmael is born; Abram is eighty-six.
kw: Mal’ak means messenger. In the older stories the angel of the Lord is often hard to tell apart from the Lord himself: in v. 13 Hagar names “the Lord who spoke to her”. It is God's own presence, turned toward a person.

The name means “God hears”. The reason follows at once: the Lord has given heed to her ‘ŏnî, her affliction, the word that recalls how she was treated in v. 6. The POC has രോദനം, her cry, which brings out the same point from another side. Each time the boy's name is spoken, it will say what God did.
Usually understood as “God who sees me” or “God of seeing”. The Hebrew of v. 13 is difficult, and translations differ, but the sense of seeing is plain.
vv: Hagar, slave-girl of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?
He is the first to call her by name. God asks a question, as he asked Adam, not because he lacks knowledge but so that she can speak. Hagar has not spoken until now.
Now you have conceived and shall bear a son; you shall call him Ishmael

This is the form of the great birth announcements of Scripture, later used in Isaiah 7:14 and for Mary in Luke 1:31. Such a word is given here to a slave. The hard command in v. 9 to go back stands beside it: the text does not defend slavery. It shows God caring for a woman inside a world that is unjust, and later he will care for her and her son in the wilderness again (21:17–19).
So she named the Lord who spoke to her, “You are El-roi”

It is a remarkable thing: a foreign slave woman gives God a name of her own, and Scripture keeps it. As for the “wild ass of a man” in v. 12, the phrase is a picture of an untamed life in the open desert (see Job 39:5–8), not a judgment on any people. God promises to bless Ishmael (17:20).
ch: When God calls Moses he says, “I have observed the misery of my people” (Exodus 3:7), and in the Magnificat Mary sings that he “has looked with favor on the lowliness of his servant” (Luke 1:48). The God of Hagar is the same God. The Catechism forbids every act that leads to the enslavement of human beings (CCC 2414), and it says that those oppressed by poverty are the object of a preferential love on the part of the Church (CCC 2448). Hagar's name for God is a call to the Church to see those whom others do not see.

r.h: Before others and before the angels
set: Jesus is speaking to his disciples (12:1), and has just told them not to fear those who can kill the body (12:4). Luke writes knowing that the first Christians were questioned before synagogue courts and civil rulers alike; Acts shows both, and many of those first witnesses were themselves Jews. Jesus is preparing his disciples for courage. He is not accusing any people.
str: vv. 8–9: acknowledging or denying the Son of Man.
v. 10: the word against the Son of Man and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.
vv. 11–12: do not worry: the Holy Spirit will teach you.
kw: To say the same thing, to declare openly; the root of the Greek word for confession of faith. It is what a witness does in public.
To speak insultingly or against someone. Here it means a settled, knowing resistance to the Spirit's work (see the question below).

The courtroom word from which “apology” in the old sense comes: a spoken defence. The disciple need not have it prepared. Peter and John, called uneducated and ordinary men, stood before the council with boldness (Acts 4:13).
vv: everyone who acknowledges me before others, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God
Two courtrooms stand side by side. A word said for Jesus in a small earthly place is answered in the highest.
but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
Peter denied the Lord and was forgiven. So the saying must mean something other than a single fall.
for the Holy Spirit will teach you at that very hour what you ought to say.

The Spirit who cannot be resisted without loss is the same Spirit who stands beside the frightened witness. Matthew has the same promise: “it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you” (10:20).
ch: The Catechism teaches that all Christians are bound to witness to the faith in word and deed (CCC 2472), and that martyrdom is the supreme witness (CCC 2473). In many lands today Christians suffer for this confession. We pray for them and for those who have wronged them.

qa: What is the sin against the Holy Spirit? Have I committed it?

The Catechism explains: “There are no limits to the mercy of God, but anyone who deliberately refuses to accept his mercy by repenting, rejects the forgiveness of his sins and the salvation offered by the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1864). St John Paul II teaches the same (Dominum et Vivificantem 46). It is not a word spoken in anger or a terrible past sin. It is the refusal of forgiveness itself. A person who fears having done this, and wants God's mercy, plainly has not. Let such a person go to Confession in peace.
study: Whom do I fail to see in my home, parish or work, as Abram's house failed to see Hagar? What would it mean to look at them with God's eyes?
Where is it hard for me to acknowledge Jesus before others? What help from the Holy Spirit do I need to ask for?

lead: The week's Genesis readings end with a new name and an everlasting covenant: “walk before me, and be blameless” (17:1). The epistle says what shapes such a life: “the word of God is living and active” (Hebrews 4:12). Jesus, closing the Sermon on the Mount, says that hearing that word is not enough; the house stands on rock only if we do it. It is a good day to remember Mar Aprem, who sang that word, Mar Theodore, who died for it, and the prophet Haggai, who called God's people to build.

set: Abram was eighty-six when Ishmael was born (16:16) and is now ninety-nine (17:1). Thirteen silent years lie between the chapters. This covenant scene repeats and deepens chapter 15. Many scholars think that it comes from a later priestly strand of tradition. It goes on in vv. 9–14 to give the sign of circumcision. Read as it stands, it shows God coming back to an old man to renew all that he promised.
str: vv. 1–2: God names himself and asks for a whole life: walk before me.
v. 3: Abram falls on his face.
vv. 4–6: the new name: ancestor of a multitude of nations.
vv. 7–8: an everlasting covenant, and the land.
kw: An ancient divine name, used especially in the patriarchal stories. Its original meaning is uncertain. Some connect it with a word for mountain. The Greek and Latin tradition understood it as the All-powerful.

Whole, complete, undivided. The same word describes an animal without blemish fit for sacrifice (Exodus 12:5). Chapter 16 shows that Abram had not lived without fault; God does not cast him off, but calls him to an undivided life.
ancestor of a multitude of nations
The Hebrew plays on the sound of Abraham and ab hămôn. The new name is a promise that an old, nearly childless man has to carry about in public.
vv: I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless.

God's self-naming comes before the demand. To walk before someone means to live in the sight of the one we serve, as a servant before his lord. Hagar has just called God the one who sees; Abram is told to live in that sight.
No longer shall your name be Abram, but your name shall be Abraham; for I have made you the ancestor of a multitude of nations.
“I have made”: the verb is in the past tense although Abraham has only one son. For God, what he has promised is as good as done.
for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you.
This is the heart of every covenant in Scripture: “to be God to you”. It is the gift of himself, even more than land or descendants.
ch: The Catechism says that God gave Abram the name that means “the father of a multitude of nations” (CCC 59). Paul calls him “the ancestor of all who believe without being circumcised” (Romans 4:11). The Second Vatican Council says that all who believe in Christ, Abraham's children according to faith, are included in his call, and it reminds us that the Church draws nourishment from the root of Israel, onto which we have been grafted (Nostra Aetate 4). Baptism also gives a new name and a new life before God.

set: These are the last words of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). A sermon that began with the Beatitudes ends with a judgment and a storm. Matthew's Jesus has given his teaching, and now he says what is to be done with it. Verse 28 is the formula that closes each of the five great discourses of this Gospel: “Now when Jesus had finished saying these things”.
str: v. 21: not those who say but those who do.
vv. 22–23: great deeds without relationship: “I never knew you.”
vv. 24–25: the wise man and the rock.
vv. 26–27: the foolish man and the sand.
v. 28: the crowds are astounded.
kw: The same word as in the Lord's Prayer: “Your will be done” (6:10). In Matthew, the one who does the Father's will belongs to Jesus' true family (12:50).
The people in v. 23 claim to have worked miracles, and yet Jesus calls what they did a breaking of the law. Charisms without obedience and charity are worth nothing (compare 1 Corinthians 13:1–3).
Both men build, and both hear the words. The storm comes on both. The only difference is doing.
vv: Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven.
Calling him Lord is right and necessary; Jesus does not reject it. He rejects it when it stands alone. “Lord, Lord” is the prayer of the bridesmaids who come too late (25:11).
I never knew you; go away from me, you evildoers.
To be known by Jesus means a bond, not information. Much religious activity can go on without it.
Everyone then who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a wise man who built his house on rock.
Jesus says “these words of mine”, placing his own teaching where Israel placed the word of the Lord. No one is promised a life with no storm.
ch: The Catechism quotes this saying when it teaches on “Thy will be done”: by prayer we can discern God's will and obtain the endurance to do it, and one enters the kingdom not by speaking words but by doing the Father's will (CCC 2826). St James says the same in plain words: “be doers of the word, and not merely hearers” (James 1:22). A Fast that does not lead to doing is only a form of saying “Lord, Lord”.

rite: Our Church today remembers Mar Aprem, St Ephrem the Syrian. Born at Nisibis about 306, he served as a deacon there and later at Edessa, where he died in 373. He taught the faith through hymns sung by choirs; he is called the Harp of the Spirit, and Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1920. He wrote of the word of God that we are like thirsty people at a spring: we take what we can and much more remains, and we should give thanks for what we received and not grieve over what we could not hold (in substance, Commentary on the Diatessaron). With him we remember Mar Theodore, a soldier who chose to die rather than deny Christ, and the prophet Haggai, who asked a people back from exile: “Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” (Haggai 1:4). One sang, one bled, one called for building, and each did what he heard.
study: God said to Abram, “walk before me”. If I lived this week remembering that God sees me, what would change?
If a storm came today, what would my house be found standing on? What word of Jesus have I heard many times and not yet done?

lead: Garbo means the leper, and on this Sunday the Great Fast looks at Christ the physician. The evening Gospel (Matthew 8:1–4) and the Gospel of the Qurbono (Luke 5:12–16) tell the same healing. The Old Testament lessons surround it. Noah goes into the ark and “the Lord shut him in” (Genesis 7:16). Jeremiah sees God's people as lost sheep coming back in tears (50:4–7). Isaiah prays, “Be our arm every morning” (33:2). Saul, newly baptized in Damascus, proclaims Jesus (Acts 9:20–25).

We study three readings that belong together. Naaman, the great general of Aram, must lay down his pride and go down into a small river. Paul says that all boasting is excluded, and that we stand before God by faith. The leper of the Gospel has nothing left to boast of, and says only, “Lord, if you choose”. Humility is the door, and the hand of Christ is on the other side of it.

r.h: Naaman goes down into the Jordan
set: The story belongs to the cycle of the prophet Elisha, in the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Aram, with its capital at Damascus, were often at war. Naaman is an enemy commander and a foreigner. Those who help him along the way are nearly all people with no rank: a captive girl, a messenger, a few servants. The powerful, the two kings and at first Naaman himself, only get in the way.
str: v. 1: Naaman's greatness, and the one word that spoils it.
vv. 2–4: the captive girl speaks.
vv. 5–7: letters, silver and gold: the king of Israel tears his clothes.
vv. 8–10: Elisha sends a messenger, not even coming to the door.
vv. 11–12: Naaman's anger.
vv. 13–14: the servants' reasoning, the washing and the healing.
kw: A broad Hebrew word for various skin diseases and even for marks on cloth and walls (Leviticus 13–14). It is not necessarily what we now call Hansen's disease. Naaman still serves as a commander, so he was evidently not cut off as the sick were in Israel.

The girl who begins the story is “a little girl” (v. 2). At the end Naaman's flesh is like that of “a little boy” (v. 14). The Hebrew uses the same two words. The great man has been brought to the size of the child who pointed him to God.
Naaman “immersed himself” seven times. The ancient Greek translation of this verse has ebaptisato, from the verb that gives us the word baptism. Seven, in the Bible, is the number of fullness.
vv: If only my lord were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would cure him of his leprosy.
A girl carried off from her home by this man's raiders wishes him well. All the healing begins with the mercy of the one who had the most reason to hate him.
I thought that for me he would surely come out, and stand and call on the name of the Lord his God, and would wave his hand over the spot, and cure the leprosy!
“For me.” Naaman has come with an idea of how God should treat a man like him. His disappointment is not with the river. It is with being treated like everyone else.
Father, if the prophet had commanded you to do something difficult, would you not have done it?
Servants who call their master “Father” teach him. It is often easier to do a hard thing than a plain one, since a hard thing lets us keep our pride.
So he went down and immersed himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God; his flesh was restored like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.
“He went down”: in body and in spirit. What heals is not the water by itself but the word of God obeyed. The verses just after say that Naaman returns and confesses the God of Israel (5:15).
ch: Jesus himself recalls this story at Nazareth: “none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:27). God's mercy goes beyond every border, and this was not a new idea but the old Scripture of Israel. The Fathers read Naaman as a figure of baptism. St Ambrose, explaining the sacraments to the newly baptized, points to Naaman's doubt about the river and teaches that it is not the water but the grace of Christ that heals (in substance, On the Mysteries). The Catechism sees the Jordan as part of the Old Testament's preparation for baptism, and Jesus himself goes down into it (CCC 1222–1224).

set: Paul writes about the year 57 or 58 to a Church he did not found, made up of Christians of Jewish and of Gentile background. In chapters 1–3 he has shown that all, Jews and Gentiles alike, need God's mercy, and in 3:21–26 he has announced God's saving righteousness through faith in Christ. Today's passage draws the conclusions. Paul speaks here as a Jew who loves his people (9:1–5), and he calls Abraham “our ancestor”.
str: vv. 27–28: boasting is excluded; we are justified by faith.
vv. 29–30: God is one, the God of Jews and of Gentiles.
v. 31: faith does not overthrow the law.
4:1–3: Abraham is the proof from Scripture.
kw: Standing before God on the basis of one's own achievement or status. For Paul it is the opposite of faith, and he allows only one boast: in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Keeping the commandments of the Mosaic Law. Many scholars think Paul is thinking in particular of what marked off Jews from Gentiles, such as circumcision and food laws; others think he means the Law as a whole, as a way of standing before God on one's own account. He does not mean Christian love and good works done by grace (see Galatians 5:6).
The Greek Old Testament's word in Genesis 15:6. It is the language of crediting, and Paul will use it again and again in chapter 4.
vv: For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works prescribed by the law.

Nothing we do earns the first gift. Martin Luther's German Bible added “alone” here, as some earlier writers had done in explaining Paul; the word is not in the Greek. Catholics and Lutherans have in our own time said together what they believe about this (see the question below).
Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also?
Paul argues from Israel's own creed: “The Lord is our God, the Lord alone” (Deuteronomy 6:4). If God is one, he is one God for all.
Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
Paul does not despise the Law. Christ is its goal, and the Spirit gives power to fulfil what it asks (8:4).
For what does the scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”
The verse comes from Genesis 15:6, before Abraham was circumcised (Genesis 17). So he is a father for all who believe (4:11).
ch: The Council of Trent itself teaches that nothing that comes before justification, neither faith nor works, merits the grace of justification (Session 6, chapter 8). The Catechism says that justification has been merited for us by the Passion of Christ (CCC 1992) and that it comes from the grace of God (CCC 1996); with regard to God, we have no strict right to any merit (CCC 2007). It quotes St Thérèse: “In the evening of this life, I shall appear before you with empty hands” (CCC 2011). In this the leper and Naaman are our teachers.

r.h: I do choose. Be made clean.
set: This follows the call of Peter (5:1–11), and the same healing appears in Mark 1:40–45 and Matthew 8:1–4. Under Leviticus the person with such a disease must cry out “Unclean, unclean” and “shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp” (13:45–46). This law was meant to guard the community, and it cost the sick person almost everything: home, worship and the touch of other human beings.
str: v. 12: the man falls down and makes his request.
v. 13: the hand, the word, the healing.
v. 14: the order: show yourself to the priest.
v. 15: the word spreads; crowds gather.
v. 16: Jesus withdraws to pray.
kw: Literally “full of leprosy”. Only Luke says this. The man has nothing left of his former life to appeal to.
if you choose / I do choose
The man does not doubt that Jesus can; his question is whether Jesus wants to. The same verb comes back in Jesus' answer. It is the real question of many who are in pain.
Jesus could have healed by a word, as he does elsewhere. He stretches out his hand first. Under the Law, touching such a person made one unclean. Here the holiness of Christ goes the other way.
vv: Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.
He says “clean”, not “well”. He asks for his whole life back: family, worship, a place among people.
Then Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said, “I do choose. Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy left him.
This man may not have felt a human touch in years. Jesus gives him that before the healing has even happened. Mark adds “Moved with pity” (1:41), and the Lord's will to heal has not changed.
for a testimony to them.

Jesus sends him to the priest, as Leviticus 14 commands. He does not set aside the Law; he honours it, and the man's healing becomes a witness. The priest's task was to confirm the cure, and so the man could go home.
But he would withdraw to deserted places and pray.
The Greek describes a habit. The more the crowds came, the more he withdrew. The physician of bodies lives from the Father's presence, and a parish that serves the sick needs the same.
ch: The Catechism calls Christ's compassion toward the sick and his many healings a resplendent sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503). It adds that he often makes use of signs, and that the sick try to touch him (CCC 1504). In the sacraments, it says, Christ continues to touch us in order to heal us (CCC 1504). He is the “physician of our souls and bodies” (CCC 1421). St John Chrysostom, preaching on the same healing, says that Jesus touched the leper to show that he was above the Law: his hand did not become unclean, but the body of the leper became clean (in substance, Homilies on Matthew 25). The Fathers often saw leprosy as an image of sin, which spreads, isolates and disfigures.

qa: Was biblical leprosy the same as Hansen's disease?

Not necessarily. The Hebrew ṣāra‘at and the Greek lepra cover a range of skin conditions. What matters in these stories is the exclusion from the community that came with it. In our time, those with Hansen's disease can be treated and cured, and they still need our welcome.
Does Paul contradict St James, who says that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:24)?

No. Paul speaks of how we first come into right relation with God, and that is by grace through faith, before any work of ours. James speaks of living faith, which must show itself in action. The Council of Trent and the Catechism hold both. In 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, saying together: by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts and equips us for good works (15). Paul himself says that what counts is “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).
Why does Jesus tell him to tell no one?

Probably because Jesus did not want to be taken as a mere wonder-worker, drawing crowds for the wrong reason. Verse 15 shows that this is just what began to happen. The command also sends the man first to the priest, so that he can return to the community by the proper way.
rite: Garbo is the Syriac word for a leper. The Sundays of the Great Fast in our tradition follow Christ the physician: the leper, the paralytic, the Canaanite woman's daughter, the bent woman, the man born blind. Naaman has a special place among us. He was a man of Aram, and Syriac, the language of our liturgy, grew from the Aramaic of that same world, a language Jesus himself spoke. In this Fast, Confession is our Jordan: a plain act, and for that very reason hard for the proud. At the Holy Qurbono the hand of Christ comes closer still. He does not only touch us; in Holy Communion he comes to dwell in us.
study: Naaman wanted to be healed in his own way. What plain, humble step have I been refusing in my own life, perhaps Confession, or asking pardon?
A captive girl began Naaman's healing. Who has been a small voice of God for me? For whom can I be that voice?
Paul says that all boasting is excluded. What do I still rely on to feel right before God?
Jesus touched the man nobody would touch. Who are the untouchable people around me, and what would it cost me to reach out my hand?

lead: In Genesis God marks Abraham's household with a sign in the flesh: belonging to God reaches the body and the whole family. Colossians turns to daily life, telling masters to be just, and all to be devoted to prayer and gracious in speech. Then Jesus speaks to people who fast and worry about food: strive first for the kingdom, because your Father knows what you need. The Fast asks the same two things, that we belong to God in the body and that we trust him for tomorrow.

r.h: A covenant carried in the flesh
set: Abraham is ninety-nine years old (17:1), and the promise of a son by Sarah is still not fulfilled. In chapter 15 God made a covenant with him. Here it is confirmed: in vv. 1–8 God says what he will do, with the new name Abraham, and in vv. 9–14 he says what Abraham and his descendants must keep.

Circumcision was known among other peoples of the ancient Near East (see Jeremiah 9:25–26). In Israel it receives a new meaning, as the sign of this covenant. Many scholars think this chapter took its final form in the priestly circles of Israel, perhaps in the time of the Exile, when circumcision and the Sabbath marked the people out among the nations.
str: vv. 9–10: the command: keep the covenant; every male is to be circumcised.
vv. 11–13: the details: on the eighth day, including those born or bought into the household.
v. 14: the one who refuses is cut off from his people.
kw: ’Ôt is the same word used for the rainbow after the Flood (Genesis 9:12–13) and for the Sabbath (Exodus 31:13). A sign is something visible that recalls an invisible bond.

The usual Hebrew phrase for making a covenant is literally “to cut a covenant”. In v. 14 the same verb gives the warning “cut off”. The one who refuses the cut of the covenant cuts himself off from it.
God's promise is meant to last through all generations (vv. 7, 13, 19). The Church teaches that God has never revoked his covenant with Israel (CCC 121).
vv: Throughout your generations every male among you shall be circumcised when he is eight days old,

Before the child can choose anything, he is already marked as belonging to God's people. The rule also reaches slaves and foreigners in the household: even at this early stage the sign is not limited to Abraham's own bloodline.
So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant.
The covenant is not only an idea in the mind. It is carried in the body, and a family hands it on. For Jewish families to this day it remains a sign of joy and fidelity.
shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant.
To belong to God is also a matter of responsibility. Scripture does not treat the sign as a mere custom.
ch: The Church reads this sign as a preparation. Paul calls Abraham's circumcision “a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith” (Romans 4:11), and Colossians 2:11–12 speaks of “the circumcision of Christ” in connection with baptism. The Catechism names circumcision among the signs of the Old Covenant (CCC 1150), and it says that the circumcision of Jesus on the eighth day was the sign of his belonging to Abraham's descendants and a prefiguring of Baptism (CCC 527). The mark in the flesh points to a new birth that reaches the heart.

set: This passage belongs to the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). Just before it, Jesus has spoken of fasting (6:16–18) and of treasure in heaven: “No one can serve two masters” (6:24). His “therefore” in v. 25 draws the conclusion. Those who have chosen God as their master need not be slaves of anxiety. He is speaking to ordinary people, for whom the next meal was often a real question.
str: v. 25: the thesis: do not worry; life is more than food.
vv. 26–27: the birds, and the uselessness of worry.
vv. 28–30: the lilies and the grass.
vv. 31–33: what the Father knows, and what comes first.
v. 34: one day at a time.
kw: The word returns again and again in this passage. It means an anxiety that divides the heart. Jesus does not forbid work or planning; the birds and the lilies are an argument about trust, not a lesson against sowing.
A word Matthew likes (see 8:26). Jesus uses it for his own disciples: they do believe, but their faith has not yet reached their daily worries.
In Matthew this means living according to God's will (5:6; 6:33). The order matters: first the kingdom and God's way, and the rest “will be given to you as well”.
vv: Look at the birds of the air; they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
Jesus calls God “your heavenly Father”. The argument rests on that name. Nobody has to convince a good father to feed his children.
And can any of you by worrying add a single hour to your span of life?

A note on the text. The Greek says literally “one cubit”, and the word for “span” can also mean stature. So the NRSV speaks of an hour of life, and the Malayalam POC keeps the cubit (മുഴം). Either way the point is the same: worry adds nothing.
But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.
This is the heart of the passage. The verse does not despise food and clothes (v. 32: “your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things”). It puts them in their right place.
Today’s trouble is enough for today.
A plain and practical word. Faith does not deny trouble; it carries one day's trouble at a time. Compare the prayer for “daily bread” in 6:11.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus asks for childlike abandonment to the providence of our heavenly Father, and it quotes these verses (CCC 305). On “daily bread” it explains that Jesus is not inviting us to idleness, but wants to relieve us from nagging worry (CCC 2830). St Augustine, commenting on the Sermon on the Mount, says that we should not preach the Gospel in order to eat, but eat in order to preach the Gospel (in substance). In the Great Fast, when we give up some food by choice, this passage teaches us why: to find out what we really live on.

qa: The reading speaks calmly about slaves. Does the Bible approve of slavery?

Genesis describes the world of its time without passing judgment on it. The Gospel slowly undermines that world: Colossians 4:1 reminds masters that they too “have a Master in heaven”. The Church now plainly condemns slavery (Gaudium et Spes 27; CCC 2414).
study: Where do I carry my faith in my body and my daily habits, and not only in my thoughts?
What is the one worry I keep going back to, and what would “strive first for the kingdom” mean for it today?

lead: God gives Sarah a new name and promises her a son, and Abraham falls on his face and laughs. Ephesians says what lies behind every such promise: “by grace you have been saved through faith”, and at once adds that we were “created in Christ Jesus for good works”. Jesus then gives the test: “You will know them by their fruits.” What God gives comes first, and in time it shows on the tree.

set: This is the last part of God's speech in chapter 17. Abram has just become Abraham (17:5) and has received the command of circumcision (17:9–14). Now the promise falls on Sarai, whose barrenness has been known since 11:30. Abraham already has a son, Ishmael, by Hagar, now thirteen years old (16:15–16; 17:25). It seems to him that God's promise has already been met in the only way still possible.
str: vv. 15–16: Sarai becomes Sarah; she will bear a son and be a mother of nations.
v. 17: Abraham falls on his face and laughs.
v. 18: his prayer for Ishmael.
vv. 19–21: God's answer: Isaac will carry the covenant, and Ishmael too is blessed.
v. 22: God goes up from him.
kw: The name means “princess”. Sarai is probably an older form of the same name. The change marks a new stage in her life with God, as with Abraham; the promised kings (v. 16) will come from her too.
The name means “he laughs” or “may he laugh”. Abraham laughs in v. 17, and the son's name will keep the memory of that laugh. Sarah's own laughter follows in 18:12 and 21:6.
The name means “God hears” (see 16:11). God answers with a play on that name: “As for Ishmael, I have heard you” (v. 20).
vv: I will bless her, and moreover I will give you a son by her.
God says “I will bless her” twice in this one verse. The promise is not given to Abraham alone. Sarah is herself chosen, and nobody can take her place.
Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed, and said to himself,
His body bows in worship while his mind does the arithmetic: a hundred years and ninety years. The Bible does not hide this.
And Abraham said to God, “O that Ishmael might live in your sight!”
A father's prayer for the son he already loves. It is not rejected. God simply has something greater in mind than Abraham dares to ask.
As for Ishmael, I have heard you; I will bless him and make him fruitful and exceedingly numerous;
The covenant line will pass through Isaac (v. 21), but God's care does not stop at its edge. The child of the slave woman is heard and blessed too.
ch: Paul sees here the model of faith: Abraham “did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body” (Romans 4:19). The Catechism teaches that against all human hope God promises descendants to Abraham, as the fruit of faith and of the power of the Holy Spirit (CCC 706). It also numbers Sarah among those holy women who prepared the way for Mary: in spite of her old age she bears a son (CCC 489). St Augustine, in The City of God, understood Abraham's laugh as the joy of one exulting and not the scorn of one who doubts (in substance).

set: The Sermon on the Mount is coming to its end. After the two ways (7:13–14), Jesus warns against false teachers, and then speaks of those who say “Lord, Lord” without doing the Father's will (7:21–23) and of the two houses (7:24–27). Every part of this ending asks the same thing: not what you say, but what you do. Matthew's community also knew Christian prophets, and needed to tell the true from the false.
str: v. 15: the warning: wolves in sheep's clothing.
v. 16: the principle and the first picture, grapes and figs.
vv. 17–18: good and bad trees.
v. 19: the end of the fruitless tree.
v. 20: the principle repeated.
kw: Israel's Scriptures already warn of those who speak in God's name without being sent (Jeremiah 23:16–22). The warning passes on to the Church.
Wolves are the danger to a flock. Paul uses the same image in his farewell at Miletus: “savage wolves will come in among you” (Acts 20:29).
In the Gospels, fruit means the whole visible result of a life: what a person does, teaches and leaves behind. Compare “the fruit of the Spirit” in Galatians 5:22–23.
vv: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.
The outer look cannot be trusted. A false teacher will not look like a wolf. He will speak the language of the flock.
You will know them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles?
Jesus gives ordinary country sense. Any farmer knows that the tree decides the fruit. The test takes time, because fruit does not come in a day.
Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
This is exactly the word of John the Baptist (3:10). It is a serious warning, addressed first to the hearer's own life. The verse does not give us permission to do the cutting ourselves.
ch: The Didache, one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, applies this same test: the false prophet and the true are to be known by their ways of living (Didache 11, in substance). The Catechism uses v. 20 for a further point: we cannot be certain of our own state by our feelings or our works, yet reflection on God's blessings in our life and in the lives of the saints offers a guarantee that grace is at work, and it cites “you will know them by their fruits” (CCC 2005).

study: What has God promised or begun in my life that I have stopped expecting, as Abraham had?
If someone looked only at the fruit of my past year, what would they say the tree was?

lead: Abraham obeys “that very day”, with no delay and no bargaining. Colossians shows where such trust is rooted: in Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”. In the Gospel, two people want to follow Jesus, but on their own terms, and Jesus tells them plainly what it will cost. The readings ask a simple question in these early weeks of the Fast: when God speaks, how long do I make him wait?

set: God has just finished speaking and “went up from Abraham” (17:22). These verses tell what Abraham does next. There is no speech and no vision, only the carrying out of God's word. Abraham's faith was already counted to him as righteousness in 15:6; here the same man acts on what he has heard, in a costly and painful way, at the age of ninety-nine.
str: v. 23: Abraham circumcises Ishmael and all the men of the household, that very day.
vv. 24–25: the ages: ninety-nine and thirteen.
vv. 26–27: the summary: father, son and the whole household together.
kw: A solemn phrase in the Hebrew. It also marks the day of entry into the ark (Genesis 7:13) and the day of the Exodus (Exodus 12:41). It tells the reader that an important day in God's plan has arrived.
The whole action is measured by the word of God. Abraham does not improve or shorten the command. Genesis uses the same kind of phrase for Noah's obedience (Genesis 6:22).
vv: he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day, as God had said to him.
The command included everyone in the house, and so does the obedience. The head of the house does not simply believe by himself. His faith shapes the life of all under his roof.
Abraham was ninety-nine years old
The age is not only a date. A man of ninety-nine has every excuse, and Isaac has not yet been born. He obeys before seeing what was promised.
That very day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised;
Ishmael receives the sign, though the covenant line will go through Isaac (17:21). Abraham treats him as his son and God's promise to him stands (17:20).
ch: Paul draws a careful lesson from the order of events: Abraham received the sign as “a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised” (Romans 4:11). Faith comes first, and obedience seals it. The Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith (CCC 144–145), and in its teaching on prayer it says that when God calls him, Abraham goes forth “as the Lord had told him”, with a heart entirely submissive to the Word (CCC 2570).

set: Matthew has placed this short scene among the mighty works of chapters 8–9. Jesus has just healed many at Capernaum (8:14–17), and he now orders a crossing of the lake; the storm follows in 8:23–27. Before the disciples get into the boat, two conversations show what it means to go with him. Luke has a fuller form of the same sayings (Luke 9:57–62).
str: v. 18: Jesus sees the crowds and orders the crossing.
vv. 19–20: a scribe offers himself, and Jesus answers.
vv. 21–22: a disciple asks for delay, and Jesus answers.
kw: A teacher and interpreter of the Law. Elsewhere in Matthew scribes often oppose Jesus, but this one comes forward with a generous offer. He calls Jesus “Teacher”; the disciple in v. 21 says “Lord”.

This is the first time the title appears in Matthew, and it is always on the lips of Jesus. Daniel's vision gives it glory: “one like a human being” who receives everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14). Here the same figure has no home. The way to that glory passes through poverty and the Cross.

The word appears twice in v. 22, which seems to play on two meanings. A common reading, already among the Fathers, takes the first “dead” to mean those who do not yet live the new life of the kingdom.
vv: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.”
It is a fine offer, and nothing suggests it is insincere. Matthew does not tell us what the scribe did next, so the question stays open for the reader.
“Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”
Jesus does not refuse him. He shows him the true price. In the Sermon on the Mount the birds were a reason to trust (6:26); here they have what Jesus himself gave up.
“Lord, first let me go and bury my father.”
To bury a parent was one of the most sacred duties in Jewish life (see Tobit 4:3). The request is good. Its one problem is the word “first”.
“Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”

This is a shocking word, and it is meant to be. When Elisha asked to kiss his parents goodbye, Elijah let him go (1 Kings 19:20). Jesus claims more than any prophet could claim. He is not abolishing the honour due to parents, which he himself defends (Matthew 15:3–6); he is saying that nothing comes before God's call.
ch: The Catechism says that family ties are important but not absolute, and that the first vocation of the Christian is to follow Jesus (CCC 2232). It also teaches that burying the dead is a corporal work of mercy (CCC 2300), so this verse cannot be turned into a rule against funerals. St John Chrysostom, preaching on Matthew, explains that Jesus is showing that nothing is more necessary than the things of heaven (in substance). The saying has been a call to those who leave home for God in every age, including those called to monastic life, to priesthood and to mission.

qa: Why does Abraham have to be circumcised, while Christians do not?

The apostles settled this at Jerusalem, deciding not to lay the burden of the Mosaic Law on Gentile believers (Acts 15:28). In Christ, “the only thing that counts is faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Baptism is the Christian's entry into the covenant (CCC 527, 1213). For Jews the sign remains a sign of the covenant that God has not revoked, and the Church speaks of it with respect (CCC 839).
study: Is there something God has clearly asked of me that I have been putting off? What would “that very day” look like?
What is the “first let me” in my own following of Jesus?

lead: Today two tables are set. Abraham runs to feed three strangers at Mamre and finds that God has come to his tent. A king prepares a wedding feast for his son, and those invited will not come. Between them 2 Corinthians says, “we are the temple of the living God”: God has chosen to dwell with us. The Fast is not the opposite of the feast. It clears a space, so that we can recognise the Guest and be ready to go in.

set: The scene comes straight after the covenant of chapter 17. Abraham lives in tents near Hebron, by the great trees of Mamre (13:18). It is the hottest part of the day, the time when nobody travels and everybody rests. In the world of the nomads and of the ancient Near East, to receive a stranger was a sacred duty; the traveller in the desert depended on it for his life.
str: v. 1: the narrator tells us what Abraham does not yet know: the Lord appears.
v. 2: three men; Abraham runs and bows.
vv. 3–5: he offers “a little” water and bread.
vv. 6–8: the great meal, prepared in haste, and Abraham stands by as they eat.
¶ The scene moves between one and three: “the Lord”, “three men”, “my lord” in the singular, and then plural verbs. Genesis does not explain it, and that has kept readers thinking ever since.
kw: ’Ēlôn means a great tree, perhaps an oak or terebinth. Such places were remembered as places of meeting with God. The POC speaks of an oak grove (ഓക്കുമരത്തോപ്പ്).
The Hebrew piles up verbs of speed: Abraham runs (vv. 2, 7) and hurries (vv. 6, 7). An old man who has just been circumcised runs in the noon heat. Love is in a hurry.
As written in the Hebrew text it can be read as a polite “my lord” or as the divine title “my Lord”. Abraham probably means the first, while the reader knows the second is also true.
vv: The Lord appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day.
God comes at an ordinary hour, to a man sitting at his door. No altar or sacrifice is mentioned, and the visit takes place through a stranger's arrival.
He said, “My lord, if I find favor with you, do not pass by your servant.
The host asks the favour, not the guest. The great Abraham, friend of God, calls himself a servant in front of three unknown travellers.
And Abraham hastened into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Make ready quickly three measures of choice flour, knead it, and make cakes.”
He promised “a little bread” (v. 5) and gives a feast: a very large amount of the best flour and a tender calf. The generous host promises little and gives much.
and he stood by them under the tree while they ate.
The head of the house waits on his guests like a servant. Christian readers can hardly miss the later scene: “I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27).
ch: The Catechism says that because Abraham believed in God and walked in his presence, he is ready to welcome a mysterious Guest into his tent, and that this remarkable hospitality foreshadows the annunciation of the true Son of the promise (CCC 2571). The Fathers read the guests in more than one way. St Justin Martyr saw the Lord with two angels (compare Genesis 19:1). St Ambrose and St Augustine saw in the three a hint of the Holy Trinity (in substance). Christians of East and West have painted this scene as the Hospitality of Abraham, most famously in the icon of Andrei Rublev. Hebrews draws the practical lesson: “some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2).

r.h: The feast and the wedding robe
set: This is the third of three parables that Jesus tells in the Temple during his last days in Jerusalem, after the two sons (21:28–32) and the wicked tenants (21:33–46). He is speaking to the chief priests and elders about their response to him. Luke has a similar parable of a great dinner (Luke 14:16–24). Matthew's form is a king's feast for his son, and only Matthew has the wedding robe.
str: vv. 1–3: the first invitation, refused.
vv. 4–6: the second invitation: some make light of it, others kill the messengers.
v. 7: the king's anger.
vv. 8–10: the invitation goes out to everyone, “both good and bad”.
vv. 11–13: the man without the robe.
v. 14: the closing saying.
kw: Israel's prophets pictured the age to come as a feast (Isaiah 25:6) and God's love for his people as a marriage (Hosea 2:19–20). Here the king's son is the bridegroom, and Jesus has already used that image of himself (Matthew 9:15).
There is no firm evidence that hosts handed out robes at the door. The point of the story is not the custom. The guest has come in without any change in himself.
This is not a warm word in Matthew. He uses it only here, for the grumbling worker (20:13), and for Judas in the garden (26:50). Each time the person addressed is in the wrong.
vv: Go therefore into the main streets, and invite everyone you find to the wedding banquet.
The refusal does not cancel the feast. God's plan goes forward, and it widens to include those nobody expected. The Church sees herself here: called from all nations.
and gathered all whom they found, both good and bad; so the wedding hall was filled with guests.
The hall contains both kinds until the king comes. Nobody earns the invitation. And the Church on earth is a mixed gathering, which should keep us humble.
and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding robe?’ And he was speechless.
Grace invites all, and it does not leave us as we were. The man has nothing to say, because he has no excuse.
For many are called, but few are chosen.
This is a warning for those who feel safe, not a calculation of how many will be saved. Semitic speech often makes its point by a strong contrast like this.
ch: St Augustine in his sermons and St Gregory the Great in his homilies on the Gospels both say that the wedding robe is charity (in substance). The Catechism calls the Eucharist the anticipation of the wedding feast of the Lamb (CCC 1329), teaches that everyone is called to enter the kingdom, which is meant for people of all nations (CCC 543), and says that the white garment of Baptism signifies that the baptised person has put on Christ (CCC 1243). It also teaches clearly that God predestines no one to go to hell (CCC 1037): the man in the parable is not shut out by the king's whim.

qa: Does the burned city in v. 7 mean God punished the Jewish people?

No such conclusion may be drawn. Many scholars think Matthew, writing after AD 70, had the fall of Jerusalem in mind, but this remains a reconstruction. The parable is told against those who refuse God's call in any age, and the man without a robe, inside the hall, is a warning to Christians. The Church firmly rejects any idea that the Jews are rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598, 839).
study: When did a stranger or an unwelcome interruption turn out to be God's visit to me?
What does the “wedding robe” mean for how I come to the Holy Qurbono this Sunday?

lead: Behind the tent flap Sarah laughs at a promise that has come too late, and the Lord asks, “Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?” Paul has staked everything on the same power, wanting to know Christ “and the power of his resurrection”. Jesus gives the promise its firmest form: “No one will snatch them out of my hand.” The same God who opened a closed womb holds his sheep, and his word does not fail.

set: The meal at Mamre (18:1–8) now reaches its purpose. The guests have eaten, and they ask for Sarah by name, although nobody has told them it. The promise that God gave Abraham in 17:15–21 is now spoken where Sarah can hear it. She is listening at the entrance of the tent, and she is old: Genesis says plainly that the time for bearing children has passed for her (18:11).
str: v. 9: “Where is your wife Sarah?”
v. 10: the promise of a son, and Sarah listening.
vv. 11–12: the narrator explains her age; she laughs to herself.
vv. 13–14: the Lord's question and the promise repeated.
v. 15: she denies it, and he answers.
kw: The root of the name Isaac (yiṣḥāq). The laugh of disbelief here will become the laughter of joy in 21:6, after the child is born. God does not take the word away; he changes what it means.

From the root meaning something beyond human power, a wonder. It is the word often used for God's mighty deeds. The Greek Old Testament puts it with the word for “impossible”, and this is echoed in the angel's word to Mary (Luke 1:37).
The exact sense of this rare phrase is debated. Many take it as “at this time next year”; literally it may mean “at the time of life” or “of reviving”. The POC renders it “in spring” (വസന്തത്തിൽ).
vv: So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, “After I have grown old, and my husband is old, shall I have pleasure?”

It is an inward laugh with a long disappointment behind it. Her words have no hatred of God in them, only the tiredness of someone who has stopped hoping. The POC takes “pleasure” as the joy of having children.
The Lord said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh, and say, ‘Shall I indeed bear a child, now that I am old?’
Compare her actual words. She also said “my husband is old”, and the Lord leaves this out. Jewish teachers noticed this long ago and saw God's care for peace between husband and wife.
Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
This is the centre of the reading, and it is a question that each reader has to answer. The Lord gives no explanation of how it will happen. He only repeats the promise.
But Sarah denied, saying, “I did not laugh”; for she was afraid. He said, “Oh yes, you did laugh.”
God does not punish her and does not let the lie stand either. It is a very gentle correction. He keeps his promise to someone who has just laughed at it and denied doing so.
ch: The Catechism numbers Sarah among the holy women who prepared the way for Mary: in spite of her old age she bears a son (CCC 489). It also teaches that only faith can embrace the mysterious ways of God's almighty power, and that Mary is the supreme model of that faith, because she believed that “nothing will be impossible with God” (CCC 273). The two scenes belong together. Sarah asks how, and laughs. Mary asks how, and says yes. Hebrews 11:11 praises the faith that received this child, and it can be read in two ways: the NRSV makes Abraham the subject, while the POC, like other versions, reads it of Sarah herself, who considered him faithful “who had promised”.

set: The scene is set in Jerusalem at the festival of the Dedication, in winter (10:22), in the Temple, in the portico of Solomon (10:23). In John, “the Jews” often means the religious authorities who oppose Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole; Jesus and his disciples are themselves Jews. They ask him to say plainly whether he is the Messiah (10:24). He answers with the image he has already used of himself, the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (10:11).
str: v. 27: the sheep: they hear, he knows, they follow.
v. 28: what he gives them: eternal life and safety.
v. 29: the Father's hand.
v. 30: “The Father and I are one.”
kw: The voice of the shepherd (10:3–4, 16). In the Bible, hearing is the beginning of belonging: “O that today you would listen to his voice!” (Psalm 95:7).

The same word used of the wolf (10:12). The danger is real, and the sheep do not protect themselves. The verse does not say that nothing will come against them; it says that nothing can take them from him.
The Greek word here is neuter: “one thing”, not “one person”. Jesus and the Father are not the same person, and yet they are one.
vv: My sheep hear my voice. I know them, and they follow me.
There are three short verbs. In the Bible “know” means a relationship, not information. The sheep do not first understand everything. They recognise a voice and they go after it.
I give them eternal life, and they will never perish.
In John, eternal life begins now, in knowing the Father and the Son (17:3). The gift is put in the present tense.
What my Father has given me is greater than all else, and no one can snatch it out of the Father’s hand.

A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts differ here. Some read as the NRSV does, “what my Father has given me is greater”. Many others read “my Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all”, and the Malayalam POC follows these (എല്ലാവരെയുംകാൾ വലിയവനാണ്). Both end at the same place: the sheep are safe in the Father's hand.
The Father and I are one.”

The opponents understand it as a claim to be God, and they take up stones (10:31–33). St Augustine notes that the word “one” answers Arius, and that the plural “are” answers Sabellius: one God, and yet not one person (in substance).
ch: The Second Vatican Council, in words quoted by the Catechism, calls the Church a sheepfold whose one and necessary door is Christ, and a flock whose sheep, though governed by human shepherds, are unfailingly nourished and led by Christ himself, the Good Shepherd (Lumen Gentium 6; CCC 754). The Fathers, above all during the Arian controversy, read v. 30 as a witness to the unity of the Father and the Son, which the Council of Nicaea confessed: “one in being with the Father”.

qa: If no one can snatch the sheep, can a Christian ever be lost?

Christ's hand is sure, and no outside power is stronger than he is. But the promise is made to those who hear and follow. The Church teaches that a person can still turn away by serious sin (CCC 1861), and she teaches us to hope and pray for the grace of final perseverance (CCC 2016). We trust the shepherd, and we keep following.
rite: The Malankara calendar today remembers Mar Ishaq. It is also the anniversary of the episcopal ordination of Joseph Mar Thomas (2005). A Gospel of the shepherd suits such a day: we pray for those who shepherd us, that they may stay close to the voice of the one Shepherd.
study: What promise of God have I met with Sarah's quiet laugh? What would it mean to let him name that laugh?
Among all the voices of my day, how do I recognise the Shepherd's? When did I last follow it?

lead: God takes Abraham into his confidence about Sodom: he has heard an outcry and will not ignore it. Titus reminds us how God has dealt with us: “he saved us, not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy”. And Jesus tells his “little flock” not to be afraid, to give alms, and to put their treasure where it cannot be lost. A people who know God's mercy must also listen for the cry of the poor. Prayer, fasting and alms all belong here.

r.h: Shall I hide this from Abraham?
set: The meal at Mamre is over. The visitors leave, and Abraham walks with them, as a good host does. They look down towards Sodom in the plain, whose wickedness was mentioned as early as 13:13. Before the visitors go on, Genesis lets us hear the Lord thinking aloud. These verses prepare the way for Abraham's great prayer for the city in 18:22–33.
str: v. 16: the men set out, and Abraham goes with them.
vv. 17–19: God's reflection: why Abraham should be told.
vv. 20–21: the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah; God will go and see.
kw: Literally in v. 19, “I have known him”. The NRSV rightly renders “I have chosen him”. To be known by God is to be chosen and drawn into a relationship (compare Amos 3:2).

The great pair of the prophets (Isaiah 5:7; Amos 5:24). Abraham is chosen so that a people may be formed who live in this way. The blessing for the nations (v. 18) will come through a people who do justice.
A word used for the cry of those who suffer wrong: it is the word used of Israel crying out in Egypt (Exodus 3:7). The word tells us that Sodom's sin has victims, and God hears them.
vv: The Lord said, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,

God speaks almost as a friend does. Scripture calls Abraham God's friend (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23), and Amos says, “Surely the Lord God does nothing, without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). Jesus takes up the same thought: “I have called you friends” (John 15:15).
No, for I have chosen him, that he may charge his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord by doing righteousness and justice;
This verse describes the Christian home as well. Abraham's great vocation here is to pass on the way of the Lord to his children. Faith that is not handed on to children stops with one generation.
“How great is the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah and how very grave their sin!

Genesis 19 shows violence against strangers. Ezekiel gives a further charge: “pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). After the hospitality of Abraham, the contrast is strong.
I must go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me;
God knows everything, and Genesis speaks in human terms, as at Babel (11:5). The picture teaches that God's judgment is careful and fair. He does not condemn on rumour.
ch: The Catechism names “the sin of the Sodomites” among the sins that cry to heaven, along with the blood of Abel, the cry of the people oppressed in Egypt, the cry of the foreigner, the widow and the orphan, and injustice to the wage earner (CCC 1867). It also teaches that since Abraham, intercession, asking on behalf of another, has been the mark of a heart attuned to God's mercy (CCC 2635). So God shares this with Abraham in order to teach him to pray: he who hears the cry of the victims wants a friend who will stand before him for others.

set: Jesus is on the journey to Jerusalem, teaching his disciples. He has just told the parable of the rich fool (12:13–21) and has said much the same as Matthew's words on the birds and the lilies (12:22–31). These three verses draw the conclusion: if the Father will give you the kingdom, you can afford to be generous with what you have.
str: v. 32: the promise: fear not; the kingdom is yours.
v. 33: the command: sell, give, store up in heaven.
v. 34: the reason: the heart follows the treasure.
kw: The phrase is only found here. It is a tender name for a small, threatened group. Behind it stands the Old Testament image of God as shepherd of his people (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34:15).
God's giving is not reluctant or forced: he is pleased to give. The kingdom is a gift before it is a task.
In the Bible the heart is not only the place of feeling. It is the centre of the person, where decisions are taken (see CCC 2563).
vv: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
The command that follows, “sell”, rests on this verse. People who are afraid hold on tight. People who know they have been given the kingdom can open their hands.
Sell your possessions, and give alms.

Jesus is not just giving good advice about money. In Luke, what we do with possessions shows what we believe. Alms are a form of worship. Tobit and Sirach had already taught this (Tobit 4:7–11; Sirach 3:30).
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

Note the order. We might expect him to say that our money follows our heart, but he says the heart follows the money. It is a good test: look at the accounts of a household, and you can see what it loves.
ch: The Catechism says that Scripture and the Fathers insist above all on three forms of penance, fasting, prayer and almsgiving (CCC 1434). It teaches that Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544). And it quotes St John Chrysostom: “Not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life. The goods we possess are not ours, but theirs” (CCC 2446). In the Great Fast, what we save by fasting is meant to reach those who go hungry without choosing to.

qa: Must every Christian sell everything?

Some are called to do so literally, as monks and religious have done. Not everyone is. In Luke, Zacchaeus gives half (Luke 19:8), and the first believers shared as any had need (Acts 2:44–45). But every Christian is called to detachment, and to share with those in need (CCC 2544–2547). The question each person must ask is what God is asking of me now, and how much of my heart my goods are holding.
study: How is my home handing on “the way of the Lord” to the next generation? What do my children or younger relatives actually see?
If someone read my bank statement or my diary for this Fast, where would they say my heart is?

lead: The Sundays of the Great Fast in the Malankara Church pass from one healing to the next: last Sunday the leper, today the paralytic, and then the Canaanite woman, the bent woman and the blind. This Sunday asks what the deepest paralysis is, and who can lift it. Ezekiel shows people who enjoy the prophet's voice like a love song and never stir themselves to act. Paul says that Christ died for us “while we still were sinners”, when we could do nothing for ourselves. Mark shows four friends digging through a roof, and a Lord who begins with forgiveness and ends with a man walking home.

The other readings of the day stand around these. The evening Gospel gives Luke's account of the same miracle (Luke 5:17–26). In Deuteronomy, Moses teaches Israel a song that will stand as a witness against forgetfulness (Deuteronomy 31:19–30). Sirach counsels us to choose our companions wisely, with “Do not abandon old friends” (Sirach 9:10–18). Isaiah cries out against those “who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:18–25). In Acts, the people carry their sick into the streets on cots and mats, so that Peter's shadow may fall on them (Acts 5:12–16). The key words today are hearing, forgiveness and rising.

r.h: They hear your words, but they will not do them
set: Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon with the exiles of 597 BC (Ezekiel 1:1–3). For years he warned that Jerusalem would fall, and his own mouth was strangely closed. Just before this reading a fugitive arrives with the news, “The city has fallen”, and Ezekiel's mouth is opened (33:21–22). What he had said has come true, and the people have to decide what they will do with his words now.

The passage looks in two directions. In vv. 23–29 the prophet speaks about those left among the ruins in the land of Israel, who claim the land by appealing to Abraham. In vv. 30–33 he speaks of his fellow exiles in Babylon, who have suddenly become eager to hear him.
str: vv. 23–24: the survivors' argument: Abraham was one man, and we are many.
vv. 25–26: the answer: look at how you are living.
vv. 27–29: the land will become a desolation.
vv. 30–32: the exiles come to hear Ezekiel as one goes to hear a singer.
v. 33: when it comes, they will know a prophet was among them.
¶ Both halves of the reading make the same point. Some rely on a famous ancestor, others on a fine sermon, and God asks both for a changed life.
kw: God's usual way of addressing Ezekiel. The NRSV gives “Mortal”; the Malayalam POC keeps “son of man” (മനുഷ്യപുത്രാ). Here it stresses the prophet's lowliness before God. It also helps the Malayalam reader to hear today's Gospel, although in Mark the title has the further background of Daniel 7:13–14.
The same word appears in v. 31 (NRSV “flattery”) and v. 32 (“love songs”). These people have made God's word into an entertainment: pleasant, moving and of no consequence.
Profit got by dishonest means. In the Hebrew their heart “goes after” their gain. The ears are in the assembly, and the heart is in the marketplace.
vv: “Abraham was only one man, yet he got possession of the land; but we are many; the land is surely given us to possess.”

It sounds like faith, and it is really a claim. They quote the promise and forget the obedience. All this past week the Genesis readings have shown that Abraham's faith was an obedience. John the Baptist will say something similar: “Do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our ancestor’” (Matthew 3:9). The warning applies to every believer: to be baptised and to have Christian grandparents is not yet to live the Gospel.
“Come and hear what the word is that comes from the Lord.”
This is what any preacher would like to hear. People are talking about his preaching by the walls and at the doors. But popularity proves nothing.
and they hear your words, but they will not obey them.
The Hebrew turns on two verbs, to hear and to do, as in Israel's own words at Sinai (Exodus 24:7). They sit “as my people” and look exactly like the faithful.
To them you are like a singer of love songs, one who has a beautiful voice and plays well on an instrument;
A very modern picture. A person can love sermons, music and beautiful liturgy, and go home unchanged.
then they shall know that a prophet has been among them.
The same words were said at Ezekiel's call (2:5). God's word does its work whether or not the audience takes it in. And it is better to learn this before events prove it.
ch: The Catechism says of Jesus' parables that “Words are not enough, deeds are required” (CCC 546). Our Lord says the same: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven” (Matthew 7:21), and James says: “be doers of the word, and not merely hearers who deceive themselves” (James 1:22). The Second Vatican Council gives this warning to preachers too, quoting St Augustine: ministers of the word must hold fast to the Scriptures by sacred reading and careful study, lest any of them become an empty preacher of the word outwardly who is not a listener inwardly (Dei Verbum 25).

set: Paul writes to the Christians of Rome, a community he has not yet visited, probably from Corinth in the second half of the 50s AD. In chapters 1–4 he has shown that all, Jews and Gentiles alike, need God's grace, and that we are put right with God through faith, with Abraham as the great example (chapter 4). Chapter 5 opens a new stage: what does life look like for those who have been justified? Paul's answer is peace, hope and a love that reaches us when we least deserve it.
str: vv. 1–2: peace and access to grace, through Christ.
vv. 3–5: suffering, endurance, character, hope; God's love poured out.
vv. 6–8: Christ died for the weak, the ungodly, the sinners.
vv. 9–10: an argument from the greater to the lesser: “much more surely”.
v. 11: we boast in God, through whom we are reconciled.
kw: A word for being brought into the presence, as of a king or into a sanctuary (see also Ephesians 2:18; 3:12). Christ brings us in by the hand. We do not force the door, and we do not have to stand outside it.
This verb runs through the passage (vv. 2, 3, 11). Paul had condemned boasting in one's own achievements (3:27). Now he says that there is a right boasting: in hope, in suffering, and in God himself.
The quality of something that has been tested and proved, like metal in the fire. The NRSV gives “character”; the POC gives courage of spirit (ആത്മധൈര്യം).
Words from everyday relations between people: enemies being made friends (v. 10). God is the one who takes the first step (see 2 Corinthians 5:18–19).
vv: Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

A note on the text. The ancient manuscripts differ by one letter in Greek. Many read “we have peace”, as the NRSV does. Others, including some of the oldest, read “let us have peace”, and the Malayalam POC follows that sense (സമാധാനത്തിൽ ആയിരിക്കാം). Taken together they say that peace is God's gift, and that we are to live in it.
And not only that, but we also boast in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance,

Paul is not saying that suffering is good in itself. He knows from experience (2 Corinthians 11:23–28) that in Christ it can bear fruit. The chain leads to hope, and for that reason suffering does not have the last word.
and hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.

Chapter 8 of the letter will develop this gift of the Holy Spirit. St Augustine returns to this verse again and again. “Poured” is a word for abundance, and the Greek tense tells of a gift already given that remains.
But God proves his love for us in that while we still were sinners Christ died for us.
This is the heart of the Letter. God does not wait until we have improved. The love comes first and the change comes from it. This is exactly what happens to the man on the mat in today's Gospel.
For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more surely, having been reconciled, will we be saved by his life.
If God did the hard part for his enemies, what will he not do for his friends? His life, as well as his death, saves us: the risen Lord is alive and at work.
ch: The Catechism cites v. 8 to teach that God's plan for us is one of benevolent love, prior to any merit on our part (CCC 604). It quotes v. 5 to say that love is God's first gift, containing all others (CCC 733). No one can merit the initial grace of forgiveness and justification (CCC 2010). In the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), Catholics and Lutherans say together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work and not because of any merit on our part, we are accepted by God (n. 15). It is a joy to hear these words shared across a very old division.

set: This is the first of five conflict stories in Mark (2:1–3:6), which end with a plot against Jesus' life (3:6). Up to now Jesus has healed and taught in Galilee, and his fame has spread (1:45). Back at Capernaum he is “at home”, perhaps in the house of Simon (1:29).

A simple house in Galilee had a flat roof, reached by an outside stair, and made of beams and branches packed with earth. So one could literally dig through it, as Mark says. Luke, writing for readers elsewhere, speaks of “tiles” (Luke 5:19), and Malayalam readers will recognise that picture too. It would not be a quiet entrance: dust and earth must have fallen on the crowd while Jesus was speaking.
str: vv. 1–2: the crowded house; Jesus is speaking the word.
vv. 3–4: the four men and the roof.
v. 5: “Son, your sins are forgiven.”
vv. 6–7: the scribes' unspoken question.
vv. 8–10: Jesus answers: which is easier?
vv. 11–12: the man stands and goes, and all glorify God.
¶ The healing story (vv. 3–5, 11–12) is broken open by the argument about forgiveness (vv. 6–10). So the form of the story itself says that the two cannot be separated.
kw: A poor person's bed, light enough to carry. The Malayalam POC says കിടക്ക. At the start the mat carries the man, and at the end the man carries the mat.
A tender word that Jesus uses for a grown man. The first word the paralytic hears is that he belongs.
A passive verb. In Jewish reverence the passive could be a way of speaking of what God does. Here Jesus says that it is happening now, and his next words claim the authority to do it himself.
The same word that amazed the people at Capernaum in 1:22 and 27. It is the power and right to act, given by God. And it is “on earth” (v. 10): God's forgiveness has arrived in a house in Capernaum.
This is the first use of the title in Mark. Daniel saw “one like a human being” to whom was given everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14). Jesus now uses this authority to forgive a poor man on a mat.
vv: Then some people came, bringing to him a paralyzed man, carried by four of them.
We never learn their names. Each of them has a corner of the mat. This is what intercession looks like, and it is also a picture of a parish.
When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.”

“Their” faith. Faith can be seen, here as a hole in a roof. It seems that the faith of others can carry one who cannot walk by himself, as the Church does for an infant at Baptism. And the man who came for his legs is given more than he had asked for.
“Why does this fellow speak in this way? It is blasphemy! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”

Their theology is correct. Only God can forgive sins. The Greek “God alone”, literally “God who is one”, recalls the great confession of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4). The scribes reason as careful teachers of the Law, and they arrive exactly at the right question. Mark leaves us to answer it.
Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Stand up and take your mat and walk’?
Either is easy to say. The second can be checked by everyone in the room. Jesus allows the visible healing to bear witness to the invisible one.
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins … “I say to you, stand up, take your mat and go to your home.”
Three commands, and the man obeys all three. He is sent home, back into his family and his village, restored in body, in soul and in his place among people.
so that they were all amazed and glorified God,
Everyone, Mark says. The story ends in praise, not in winning an argument. Today's reading never tells us what the four friends said, or whether they repaired the roof.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus gave scandal above all when he identified his merciful conduct toward sinners with God's own attitude, and when he forgave sins (CCC 589). It teaches that only God forgives sins, and that since he is the Son of God, Jesus can say of himself that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive (CCC 1441). And it opens its teaching on the sacraments of healing with this very scene: “The Lord Jesus Christ, physician of our souls and bodies, who forgave the sins of the paralytic and restored him to bodily health”, has willed that his Church continue his work of healing and salvation, in Penance and in the Anointing of the Sick (CCC 1421). St Ambrose, commenting on Luke's account, marvels at a Lord who pardons some for the sake of others' merit (in substance).

qa: Does this story mean that sickness is a punishment for sin?

No. Jesus says plainly of the man born blind, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). The Catechism notes the mysterious link of illness with sin and evil that Israel experienced, and says that God's forgiveness begins the healing (CCC 1502). In this story Jesus goes to the deepest need, but he does not say that the man's illness came from his sins. Nobody should tell a sick person that God is punishing them.
If only God can forgive, how can a priest give absolution?

Because Christ himself willed to share this ministry. On the evening of Easter he breathed on the apostles and said, “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them” (John 20:23). He entrusted the exercise of the power of absolution to the apostolic ministry (CCC 1442), and bishops and priests forgive in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1461). The priest does not forgive by his own power. The crowd in Matthew's account glorified God for giving “such authority to human beings” (Matthew 9:8).
If we are justified by faith as a gift, why do we fast?

Not to earn what has already been given. We fast as a response to it, and to open ourselves to receive more of it. The Catechism says that Jesus' call to conversion aims first at the conversion of the heart, and that without this, penances remain sterile and false (CCC 1430–1431). After the initial grace, moved by the Holy Spirit, we can grow in grace and charity (CCC 2010). So the Fast is the love of Romans 5:5 finding its way into the body.
rite: The Malankara calendar today also remembers Mar Eustathios, Patriarch of Antioch, and it is the name-day of Kuriakose Mar Eusthathios. In the West Syriac tradition of the Malankara Church, several Sundays of the Great Fast are named for those who came to Christ for healing, and M'shario takes its name from the paralytic. The Fast thus appears as a time of healing, not only of self-denial.
