The Holy Qurbono itself is full of prayers for the forgiveness of debts and sins, and this is a good Sunday to hear them as the words of Jesus to the man on the mat. It is also a good time to go to Confession, to seek the Anointing for those who are seriously ill, and to ask a practical question: who is there in our parish, among the elderly, the housebound or those who have drifted away, who cannot get to Christ unless four of us carry them?
study: Ezekiel's hearers loved his voice. What in my religious life do I enjoy without letting it change me?
Paul says that Christ died for us “while we still were sinners”. Do I act as if God loves me only when I have improved?
Whom am I carrying to Christ? Who carried me?
What is the paralysis in me, the thing that keeps me on the mat, and what would it be to hear “Son, your sins are forgiven” in the sacrament of Confession this Fast?

lead: Our Church keeps today the feast of the See of St Peter at Antioch, in the third week of the Great Fast. The three readings together draw a portrait of the one who is given charge of God's people. In Genesis, Abraham stands before the Lord and pleads for a city that is not his own. In Hebrews, the believers are told to remember those who led them, and to hold on to the one Lord who does not change when leaders pass away. In Matthew, a slave is put in charge of a household to feed the others at the proper time, and must answer for how he did it. The key words are standing before God, remembering and feeding: this is the feast of a ministry, of which the chair is the sign.

set: The scene follows straight on from Mamre, where Abraham welcomed three visitors and heard the promise of a son (18:1–15). As the visitors leave, the Lord decides not to hide from Abraham what he is about to do. He has heard a great outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah, and he will go down to see (18:20–21). The word “outcry” is the cry of people who suffer wrong.

Abraham's nephew Lot lives in Sodom (13:12), but Abraham never mentions him. He pleads for the whole city, and his question is about God's own justice. May the righteous be swept away with the wicked? Then the question grows: may the few righteous save the many who are not?
str: v. 22: the men go on toward Sodom; Abraham stays before the Lord.
vv. 23–25: the bold question about justice.
vv. 26–32: six requests, from fifty down to forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty and ten; each is granted.
v. 33: the Lord goes his way; Abraham returns to his place.
¶ Abraham is the one who stops counting. The text never says that God refused him.
kw: A person who is in right relationship with God and neighbour. Later in Genesis the same word is used by the king of Gerar, in 20:4.
A title that reaches past Israel to the whole world. Abraham appeals to God against the fear that God might act unjustly, and in so doing he confesses who God is.
A rhyming pair in Hebrew, found also in Job 30:19 and 42:6. It names the creature's lowliness and mortality. Abraham's boldness never forgets it.
vv: while Abraham remained standing before the Lord.

Ancient Jewish scribal lists count this verse among places where the wording was changed out of reverence, so that it once said that the Lord remained standing before Abraham. Scholars discuss how far these lists are reliable as history, but the tradition itself shows how astonishing the scene seemed: God waits for the man to speak.
Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
This is prayer, not rebellion. Abraham holds God to what God has shown himself to be. Only someone who trusts God's justice can ask this.
Let me take it upon myself to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes.
Humility and courage appear in one sentence. The prayer of the Bible does not choose between them.
For the sake of ten I will not destroy it.
God's answer never falls short of the request. Abraham's prayer begins to show something that Jeremiah 5:1 and Isaiah 53 will carry further: a few, or even one, may stand for many.
ch: The Catechism says that Abraham's heart is attuned to his Lord's compassion for men and that he dares to intercede for them with bold confidence (CCC 2571). Christian intercession is a sharing in the prayer of Jesus, “the one intercessor with the Father on behalf of all men” (CCC 2634). The Church reads the shrinking numbers in the light of the one righteous man, of whom Paul writes: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). On a feast of Peter this reading says what a shepherd does first of all: he stands before God for his people.

r.h: Remember your leaders; the Lord does not change
set: The letter does not name its author, and calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). It seems to be addressed to Christians who had grown tired under pressure. Chapter 13 gathers its closing practical advice.

The leaders in verse 7 seem to be people who have already died, since their “outcome” can now be looked at. The first generation is passing, and new teachings are going about (13:9). The writer's answer is the sentence in the middle: Jesus Christ does not pass.
str: v. 7: remember those who spoke the word of God, and imitate their faith.
vv. 8–9: Christ the same; do not be carried away by strange teachings.
vv. 10–14: an altar, the sacrifice outside the gate, and the city to come.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifices that remain: praise, doing good, and sharing.
kw: “Those who lead”, a plain word and not a title of rank, used three times in this chapter (13:7, 17, 24). Here their leading consists in speaking God's word and in a life worth copying.
The Greek Old Testament uses this phrase for an offering of thanksgiving, as in Psalm 50. Here it is offered “through him”, through Christ.
Translated “to share what you have” in verse 16. It is the word for fellowship and for what the first Christians held in common (Acts 2:42). Hebrews names it, too, as a sacrifice.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
The Church's memory of her leaders is not nostalgia. The point of remembering them is to do what they did: to believe.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Leaders die and teachings change, but the one they preached does not. Every ministry in the Church, Peter's included, lives only by serving him.
We have an altar

Scholars discuss whether the writer is thinking first of the Cross or of the Eucharist. The Letter's own argument centres on the sacrifice of Christ, and the Church, feeding on that sacrifice, has not been wrong to hear in this line the altar of her own worship.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.

The writer sees a sign in the bodies of the sin offerings burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). His aim is to draw tired Christians toward Christ, not to speak against Israel, whose Scriptures he is using to think with.
Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
Together with verse 16, this ties worship and generosity into one offering. In the Great Fast, prayer and giving to others belong together.
ch: The Catechism uses verse 15 when it lists the names of the Eucharist, among them “the sacrifice of praise” (CCC 1330). For the Church's understanding of leadership, the feast points to Antioch itself. It was from that Church that St Ignatius of Antioch was led away to martyrdom at Rome. In his letters he urged the Christians to stay united with their bishop, and he is the first we know of to use the phrase “the Catholic Church” (To the Smyrnaeans 8).

r.h: The slave put in charge of the household
set: These verses come near the end of the long discourse on the Mount of Olives (chapters 24–25). Jesus has just said that no one knows the day or the hour (24:36). Now he tells a series of parables about the time of waiting.

In Luke's version of the same saying, Peter is the one who asks, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for everyone?” (Luke 12:41). The answer there, as here, concerns someone given charge over others. This explains why the parable suits a feast of Peter, though it speaks to everyone with any responsibility for others: parents, teachers, employers and clergy.
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise slave?
vv. 46–47: the blessing on the one found at work.
vv. 48–49: the other way of using the time.
vv. 50–51: the unexpected return and the judgement.
kw: Phronimos is practical good sense, the wisdom of the bridesmaids with oil in the next chapter (25:2). Faithfulness and common sense are asked for together.
The food comes when it is needed. A good steward does not feed people when it suits him.
In Greek, originally a stage actor. The wicked slave plays at being a steward while he uses the position for himself.
vv: Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
He remains a slave among slaves. He is not the owner of the house. Authority here is defined by the food it gives.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
Readiness for the Lord's return is not anxious watching of the sky. It means being found doing the work given to you.
and he begins to beat his fellow slaves, and eats and drinks with drunkards,
Two sins of those in charge are named: harshness to those under them, and self-indulgence at their expense.
He will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites,
A fierce image in the style of parable. It is not a description to be taken literally, but its weight is real: responsibility for others will be answered for.
ch: The Catechism says that the office given to the pastors of God's people is in the strict sense of the term a service (CCC 1551). St Augustine told his people: for you I am a bishop, with you I am a Christian; the first is a danger and the second a grace (Sermon 340, in substance). St Gregory the Great called himself “servant of the servants of God”, and the popes have kept the title. Peter himself was given the same charge three times: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

qa: What is the See of St Peter at Antioch, and was Peter really there?

The New Testament places Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2:11), the city where the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26). Early writers such as Origen and Eusebius connect him with the beginnings of the Church there. The New Testament does not say what title he held or how long he stayed, and we should not claim to know more than that. A “see” or “throne” is the bishop's chair, the sign of his office of teaching. The feast honours Peter's ministry at Antioch; it is not in competition with his see at Rome. The Catechism teaches that the Pope, as Peter's successor, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful (CCC 882).
Did Abraham change God's mind?

Genesis tells the story in human terms, as a bargaining, and it wants us to feel the boldness of it. But the Lord himself begins the conversation, by not hiding his plan from Abraham (18:17), and he never refuses. The story shows a God who wants to be asked, and who draws a human being into his own mercy. Prayer does not teach God to be merciful. It teaches us to want what he wants.
Why does it stop at ten?

The text does not explain it. Abraham simply stops asking, perhaps out of reverence. The next chapter shows that fewer than ten were found, yet “God remembered Abraham” and brought Lot out (19:29). Abraham's prayer did more than he knew.
rite: Our Syro-Malankara Church prays in the Antiochene, West Syriac tradition, and in full communion with the Bishop of Rome. This feast joins these two sides of our identity: the Apostle who taught at Antioch is the one whose ministry continues at Rome. Our sister Churches of the Syriac tradition also honour the Antiochene see, and today is a good day to pray for the unity of all who look to Peter's confession. The Panchangam also remembers Thomas Mar Dioscoros (1943) and the anniversary of the consecration of St Mary's Cathedral, Thiruvananthapuram (1965), so that the universal and the local are held together in one day's prayer.
study: Abraham prays for a city he does not belong to. For whom, outside my own circle, do I pray in this Fast?
Who spoke the word of God to me? What in their faith can I imitate this week?
Hebrews 13:15–16 joins praise and sharing as sacrifices. How do these two come together in the way I take part in the Holy Qurbono?
In what place am I “put in charge” of others? What is the food they need from me at the proper time?

lead: The Genesis reading follows the two messengers into Sodom, where a guest is welcomed by one man and threatened by a whole town. In the Gospel, Jesus opens his own door: “Come to me.” The Epistle (Romans 5:1–5) gives the reason a yoke can be carried through suffering: “hope does not disappoint us”. The Church also remembers Mar Polycarp, who carried that yoke for a lifetime.

r.h: Lot and the guests at Sodom
set: The reading is deliberately set against the previous chapter. Abraham welcomed visitors at noon by his tent (18:1); Lot welcomes them at evening in the gate of the city. Hospitality to a stranger was a sacred duty in the ancient Near East: once a guest came under your roof, you answered for his safety. Sodom now shows its own face in how it treats a stranger.
str: vv. 1–3: Lot's welcome.
vv. 4–9: the crowd at the door; Lot's terrible offer; the threat to Lot himself.
vv. 10–11: the guests rescue their host.
kw: The ordinary Hebrew word for knowing, and also a way of speaking of sexual relations (as in 4:1). The context, including Lot's reply, shows that this is what the crowd means here: a threatened assault on the guests.
A rare word, found elsewhere only in 2 Kings 6:18. It suggests a dazzling confusion. Those who would not see the stranger as a guest cannot now even find the door.
vv: But he urged them strongly; so they turned aside to him and entered his house;
Lot has taken up Abraham's way of welcome. Everyone else in the story is about to fail where he has done well.
both young and old, all the people to the last man,
The writer stresses that the whole town is present. This also answers Abraham's question from Genesis 18: there are not ten.
for they have come under the shelter of my roof.

Lot's reason is the law of hospitality, but his offer of his own daughters is a grave wrong, and Scripture reports it without approving it. It shows how the violence of a place can bend even a person who is trying to do right.
But the men inside reached out their hands and brought Lot into the house with them,
The host who tried to protect his guests is protected by them. Lot is rescued by the very ones he thought he was saving.
ch: The Letter to the Hebrews recalls such stories when it says, “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). St Clement of Rome says that Lot was saved from Sodom on account of his hospitality and godliness (First Letter 11, in substance). The Second Letter of Peter calls him “righteous” (2:7). The Church takes the story, for all its darkness, as a call to protect the stranger and the one who has no defender.

set: These three verses are found only in Matthew. They follow Jesus' prayer of thanks that the Father has revealed these things to infants, and his claim that no one knows the Father except the Son (11:25–27). Sirach had written of Wisdom calling people to her and of putting one's neck under her yoke (Sirach 51:23–27). Jewish teachers also spoke of the yoke of the Law, and they meant a yoke to be loved. Jesus now speaks as Wisdom herself speaks.
str: v. 28: the invitation and the promise.
v. 29: the yoke and the teacher.
v. 30: why the yoke can be carried.
kw: The wooden frame that joins an animal to its load. It is an image of discipleship and of obedience. Jesus does not abolish the yoke. He offers his own.
The word of the third beatitude (5:5), and of the king who comes riding on a donkey (21:5). It is strength without violence.
More exactly, good, kind, well fitting. It does not mean that discipleship costs nothing, but that this yoke fits the one who wears it.
vv: Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
He does not tell people to come to a place or a doctrine, but to himself. The invitation has no entrance test except weariness.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
The last words echo Jeremiah 6:16. This is the only place where Jesus directly describes his own heart in the Gospels. Disciples are those who learn this heart.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
St Augustine explains that love makes light what is hard in itself (Sermon 70, in substance). The burden is not removed, but one no longer carries it alone.
ch: The Catechism quotes this saying to teach that the Word became flesh to be our model of holiness (CCC 459). In the Great Fast it is a safeguard against turning penance into a burden we bear to impress God. The fasting of a disciple is done beside a gentle Master, and is yoked to him.

qa: What was the sin of Sodom?

This reading shows a whole town ready to assault two strangers, a violent attempt at rape and a violation of guests. Elsewhere Scripture names other things as well. Ezekiel says that Sodom had “pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49), and Jude 7 speaks of “sexual immorality” and “unnatural lust”. The Catechism lists Genesis 19 among the Scriptures behind its teaching that homosexual acts are contrary to the natural law (CCC 2357), and goes on at once to say that persons with such tendencies must be accepted with respect, compassion and sensitivity (CCC 2358). So a faithful reading neither reduces this story to one thing nor uses it to despise anyone.
rite: Mar Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, is one of the living links with the Apostles. St Irenaeus, who heard him as a boy, says that he was taught by Apostles (Against Heresies 3.3.4). He died about the year 155 (some scholars date it later). The account of his martyrdom, written by his own Church, tells how he refused to curse Christ, saying that for eighty-six years he had served him and had never been wronged (in substance). He had found the yoke light indeed.
study: Who are the strangers at my door in this Fast, and how would they say they have been treated?
Jesus says, “learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart”. Where do I most need to learn this?

lead: Today's two main readings show two kinds of hesitation. Lot knows he must leave, and lingers, and God's mercy takes him by the hand. Herod knows John is right, and keeps his oath and his face instead of the truth. The Epistle (Romans 3:10–20) sets all of us beside them: “There is no one who is righteous, not even one”. The Church also remembers the finding of the head of St John the Baptist.

set: The night of violence is over and the messengers now explain why they came. The “outcry” heard in 18:20 has reached the Lord, and the city is to be destroyed. They give Lot time to warn his family. What follows is a slow, almost painful escape, and most of the delay comes from the man being rescued.
str: vv. 12–14: the warning; the sons-in-law take it as a joke.
vv. 15–16: dawn; Lot lingers and is led out by the hand.
vv. 17–22: the command to flee to the hills; Lot begs for a little town instead, and it is granted.
kw: A rare, drawn-out verb form that sounds like what it means. The grammar of the story slows down with Lot.
Genesis says, “the Lord being merciful to him” (19:16). This is compassion that spares. It is the reason for the rescue, since Lot has done nothing to earn it at this moment.
Lot's repeated plea, “is it not a little one?” (19:20), gives the town its name, Zoar. Hebrew writers love such wordplay on names.
vv: But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting.
A warning from someone who has lived comfortably among them for years does not carry much weight. Faith that has not been lived sounds like a joke.
But he lingered; so the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the Lord being merciful to him, and they brought him out and left him outside the city.
One of the tenderest lines in Genesis. Knowing that one must leave is not yet leaving. God does not wait until Lot is brave.
do not look back or stop anywhere in the Plain;
Rescue comes with an instruction. Being taken by the hand does not end the need to walk.
is it not a little one?
Even now Lot bargains, and God allows it. This is a very human picture of someone who wants to be saved, but only partly and close to home.
ch: The Second Letter of Peter draws the lesson that “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial” (2 Peter 2:9). The Church sees here what the Catechism says of grace: the very preparation for receiving grace is already a work of grace (CCC 2001). Paul's words today say the same in another way: no human being is justified by deeds prescribed by the law, and all alike need to be taken by the hand.

r.h: The death of John the Baptist
set: Herod in this passage is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome from 4 BC to AD 39. Matthew calls him “the ruler” (tetrarch), and in verse 9 “the king”, as people commonly did.

The Jewish historian Josephus also writes of John's imprisonment and death (Antiquities 18). He says that John was held at the fortress of Machaerus and that Antipas feared his influence over the people. The Gospels stress his moral rebuke. The two accounts need not exclude each other. Josephus and the Gospels differ on the name of Herodias's earlier husband, a detail historians still discuss.
str: vv. 1–2: Herod hears of Jesus and thinks of John.
vv. 3–5: flashback: why John was imprisoned.
vv. 6–11: the birthday, the oath and the head.
v. 12: the disciples bury John and tell Jesus.
kw: John's sentence rests on the Law: Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21 forbid marrying a brother's wife in these circumstances. He said it to a ruler.
Herod is grieved, but he keeps his oath because of his guests (14:9). Jesus has taught his disciples not to swear at all (5:34–37). A rash promise here becomes a cover for murder.
vv: because John had been telling him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.”
The verb suggests that he said it more than once. John did not stop at safe sins.
The king was grieved, yet out of regard for his oaths and for the guests, he commanded it to be given;
A person may feel sorrow and still do the wrong thing, because of what others would say.
His disciples came and took the body and buried it; then they went and told Jesus.
A quiet ending. They carry their grief to the right person. The next verse says that Jesus withdrew to a deserted place, and it is the prelude to the feeding of the five thousand.
ch: The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate forerunner (CCC 523) and teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). St Bede, in a homily still read by the Church, says that John was not asked to deny Christ, only to keep silent about the truth, and yet he died for Christ, who is the truth (in substance). St John Chrysostom contrasts John in chains with Herod on his throne, and shows which of them was truly bound (in substance).

qa: What is the “finding of the head”? Do we know that the relic is genuine?

Matthew says only that the head was given to Herodias's daughter and that the disciples buried the body. Ancient Christian accounts, which differ in their details, tell of the head being found and honoured, and more than one city later claimed to have the relic. We cannot settle the history, and the Church does not ask us to. The commemoration honours the prophet who lost his head rather than his witness, and it reminds us that the Church treasures even the bodily remains of those who died for the truth.
rite: Our Antiochene tradition holds St John the Baptist in great honour, and in the Great Fast he is a fitting companion: he preached repentance, lived in the desert, and did not change his message to suit the powerful.
study: What am I lingering over in this Fast, even though I know I should leave it?
Herod was grieved, yet he did it because of the guests. Where does fear of others' opinion decide what I do?

lead: Genesis tells the end of Sodom in a few heavy verses, and then looks at it through the eyes of the man who prayed. In Matthew, Jesus warns his disciples that they go as sheep among wolves. The Epistle (2 Corinthians 4:7–15) names the strength in which they go: “we have this treasure in clay jars”. All this comes together in the memory of Blessed Rani Maria, a daughter of Kerala who was killed in 1995 for her service of the poor.

set: The sun has risen and Lot has reached Zoar. The destruction is told very briefly, without any interest in the details of suffering. The cities of the Plain are placed in the region of the Dead Sea, a land of salt and bitumen. Scholars have long searched for them, but no site has been identified with certainty, and Genesis is not interested in geology. Its concern is the meaning of what happened. The reading ends where the story began, with Abraham.
str: vv. 23–25: sunrise, sulfur and fire; the cities overthrown.
v. 26: Lot's wife.
vv. 27–28: Abraham returns to his place of prayer and sees the smoke.
v. 29: the summary: God remembered Abraham.
kw: The root that remains attached to Sodom for the rest of the Bible (for example Deuteronomy 29:23, Isaiah 13:19, Amos 4:11). The “overthrow” becomes the standard picture of judgement.
A pillar stands still and looks in one direction. The image of the woman who could not go forward gets its force from this.
In Scripture, when God remembers, he acts. The same verb is used of Noah (8:1) and of Rachel (30:22). It is a turning point in each story.
vv: Then the Lord rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven;

Nothing here celebrates the destruction. The Bible uses this as a warning, not as a spectacle. The prophets hold it up against Jerusalem as well (Isaiah 1:9–10), so no reader may read this about others only.
But Lot’s wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
She was out of the city, but her heart had not left it. The command was “do not look back” (19:17).
Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the Lord;
Abraham comes back to where he prayed, and he says nothing. Many who have prayed for others and seen a disaster will know this silence.
God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow,
Genesis does not say that God remembered Lot. Lot was saved because someone had pleaded. No intercession is wasted, even when it does not seem to be answered.
ch: Jesus himself uses this story: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32), in a warning about being unready for the day of the Son of Man. The Book of Wisdom calls the pillar “a monument to an unbelieving soul” (Wisdom 10:7). St Augustine, in the City of God, sees in her a warning that those on the way of salvation must not long for what they left behind (in substance). In the Great Fast this is a simple question: having started, where is my heart looking?

set: This is part of the discourse in which Jesus sends the Twelve out (chapter 10). At the start they are sent only to Israel (10:5–6), but these verses look further on, to governors, kings and Gentiles. Many scholars think that Matthew has gathered here sayings of Jesus in the light of what the first Christians were suffering.

The “councils” and “synagogues” in verse 17 reflect a time when the first disciples, who were themselves Jews, faced conflict with some local authorities, just as they faced Roman governors. It is no charge against the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4). The same verses warn of betrayal from within one's own family, and of hatred from all sides.
str: v. 16: the image and the double instruction.
vv. 17–20: being handed over, and the promise of the Spirit.
vv. 21–23: division and endurance.
vv. 24–25: the disciple shares the Master's lot.
kw: Akeraioi means unmixed, without guile. Disciples need good sense without cunning, and purity without naivety.
The word Matthew uses for John's arrest (4:12) and for Jesus' own betrayal (17:22; 26:2). The disciples share the same road.
To remain under a burden without running from it. It does not mean winning. It means staying.
vv: See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves;
The speaker is the Shepherd, and it is he who sends them. Their weakness is known and intended.
for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
This is a promise for those on trial, and not a reason to neglect preparation for preaching. The disciple has no need to fear being left alone at the moment of witness.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
The last word is not about how much was achieved, but about faithfulness that lasted.
A disciple is not above the teacher,
If the Master was slandered, the household should not expect praise. Suffering is not proof that something has gone wrong with the mission.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the martyr bears witness to Christ who died and rose, to whom he is united by charity (CCC 2473). Tertullian's saying, that the blood of Christians is seed, has been handed on in every age (Apology 50, in substance). The Church does not seek out enemies. She prays today for those who suffer for their faith or their service in many lands, and also for those who have wronged them.

qa: Was Lot's wife really turned to salt?

Genesis reports it as a sign, in a region where salt formations stand along the shore of the Dead Sea, and ancient readers would have seen in them a reminder of this story. The Catholic reader need not decide how such a detail came to be told. What matters is what the sacred writer teaches, and Jesus' own use of it shows that: “Remember Lot’s wife.”
rite: Blessed Rani Maria Vattalil, a Franciscan Clarist sister born at Pulluvazhy in Kerala, served the poor in Madhya Pradesh and helped landless families out of the grip of moneylenders. On 25 February 1995 she was stabbed to death on a bus near Indore by a man hired by those who resented her work. Her family forgave him, and her sister, Sr Selmy Paul, visited him in prison. The Church beatified her at Indore on 4 November 2017. In her we see the clay jar and the treasure, and the Gospel's way of ending violence.
study: When have I prayed for someone, and seen no result? What does “God remembered Abraham” say to me?
What does it mean for me to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” where I work or live?

lead: Genesis closes Lot's story in a cave, with a family cut off from everyone by fear. In Matthew, Jesus speaks of a different kind of closed room: the place where we pray to the Father in secret. The Epistle (Romans 2:1–11) warns against judging others and reminds us that “God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance”. What fear makes of us, and what the Father's nearness makes of us, are set side by side.

r.h: Lot and his daughters in the cave
set: This is the last we hear of Lot, the man who once chose the richest land (13:10–11). Now he has left Zoar out of fear and lives in a cave with what remains of his family. His daughters believe that “there is not a man on earth” left for them (19:31). They may think that the destruction has been total.

The story also explains the origin of two neighbouring peoples, Moab and Ammon, east of the Jordan. Many scholars think that it may have been told in Israel partly as an unflattering account of those neighbours. Yet Scripture also shows God caring for them. He gives them their lands, because they are the descendants of Lot (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19).
str: v. 30: from Zoar to the cave.
vv. 31–36: the daughters' plan, carried out on two nights.
vv. 37–38: two sons and two peoples.
kw: Literally “seed”, one of the great words of Genesis, tied to God's promise to Abraham (12:7; 15:5). Here the daughters try to secure offspring by their own desperate means.
Hebrew hearers would catch a sound of “from a father” in Moab, and Ben-ammi means “son of my kin”. The names carry the memory of the story's origin.
vv: for he was afraid to stay in Zoar;
Lot begged for Zoar and now flees from it. A man who has been rescued by mercy still lives as if everything depended on himself.
there is not a man on earth to come in to us
Their sin grows out of despair and isolation. The story describes it, and it does not praise it.
he did not know when she lay down or when she rose.
The man who sat in the gate and made judgements now knows nothing at all. Drink has taken the rest from him. The writer's repetition (19:35) is a quiet condemnation.
he is the ancestor of the Ammonites to this day.
The story ends without any word from God, one of the bleakest silences in Genesis. But God's story with these peoples is not finished.
ch: The Second Vatican Council says that the Old Testament books contain some things that are incomplete and temporary (Dei Verbum 15; CCC 122). A reader must not take every act told in Scripture as an example. The Church teaches clearly that incest is a grave offence (CCC 2388), and a story like this is never a reason to excuse any abuse in a family. Some Fathers, such as Origen, noted that the daughters believed no other people were left on earth (in substance), which explains their act without making it good.

Then God's mercy goes beyond the story. Ruth the Moabite becomes an ancestor of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), and Naamah the Ammonite is the mother of Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:21), who is also in Matthew's list (1:7). Nothing in human history is too broken for God to bring into his plan.

r.h: Pray to your Father in secret
set: The Sermon on the Mount takes the three works of Jewish piety in turn: almsgiving, prayer and fasting (6:1–18). All three are good and are assumed: “whenever you pray”. Jesus' question is who they are done for. The Great Fast takes up the same three works.

Standing to pray was normal among Jews, and the synagogue was a place of prayer. Jesus is not criticising them. The fault he names is the desire “to be seen by others”, and it is a fault found among religious people of every kind, not of one people.
str: v. 5: the way of those who pray to be seen.
v. 6: the room and the shut door.
vv. 7–8: not many words, for the Father knows; the Lord's Prayer then follows (6:9–13).
kw: In Greek, a stage actor. The person performs for an audience, and the audience gives the reward.
An inner room or storeroom, the kind of place that had a door that could be shut. Its plainness is part of the point.
A rare word, whose exact origin is uncertain. It suggests babbling. The error is the belief that a quantity of words can wear God down.
vv: so that they may be seen by others. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.
The Greek verb is one used for a receipt: paid in full. They wanted to be seen, and they were.
But whenever you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret;
The “you” becomes singular here. Each one must meet God alone, and the one met is a Father.
for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.
Then why ask? Prayer does not inform God. It places us before him as children, and it changes the one who asks.
ch: The Catechism says that from the Sermon on the Mount onwards Jesus insists on conversion of heart, and it names among his teachings “prayer to the Father in secret”, not heaping up empty phrases (CCC 2608). St Cyprian, writing on the Lord's Prayer, recalls Hannah, who prayed without raising her voice, as a model: God hears the heart (in substance).

qa: Does this forbid public prayer, or long prayers like our Hours and liturgy?

No. Jesus himself prayed with his people, went to the synagogue and the Temple, and taught his disciples to say “Our Father”, in the plural. The warning is about motive, and about trusting in words as a technique. St Augustine, writing to Proba, distinguishes much speaking from much praying: long prayer of the heart is good, and many words without it are not (Letter 130, in substance).
study: When has fear pushed me into a decision I would otherwise never have made? What would trust have changed?
Do I have a “room” and a time for prayer in this Fast, where no one but the Father sees?

lead: A foreign king in Genesis listens to God in a dream, while Abraham, the friend of God, tells a half-truth out of fear. The Epistle (Romans 2:12–16) then speaks of Gentiles who show that “what the law requires is written on their hearts”. In Luke, Jesus calls for open witness and promises that the Holy Spirit will teach us what to say. The readings ask whether we will speak truthfully when we are afraid, and they assure us that God is not limited to the people we expect him to work through.

set: Abraham moves south to the Negeb, and lives as an alien at Gerar. This is the second of three stories in Genesis in which a patriarch passes off his wife as his sister (12:10–20; 26:6–11). Many scholars think they are forms of an old tradition retold in different settings. As they stand, they show that faith does not remove fear overnight.

The timing makes the danger greater. Abraham has just been promised that Sarah will bear a son (18:10). If she is lost now, so is the promise. God himself steps in to protect what Abraham has put at risk.
str: vv. 1–2: Abraham's half-truth; Sarah is taken.
v. 3: God comes to Abimelech in a dream.
vv. 4–5: the king defends himself.
vv. 6–7: God answers: he knows, he has restrained him, and Abraham must pray.
kw: Wholeness, with nothing divided. A foreign king is the one who uses this phrase here, and God accepts it.
This is the first time the word appears in the Bible, and it is used of Abraham. Here the mark of a prophet is not foretelling, but that he “will pray for you”.
vv: But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night,
God speaks to a king outside the covenant. He is not bound to the boundaries that we draw.
Lord, will you destroy an innocent people?
In Hebrew the word for “innocent” is the same as Abraham's word for “righteous” in 18:23. The foreign king now asks God Abraham's own question.
furthermore it was I who kept you from sinning against me.
A striking insight: God's care lies behind even the sins we have not committed. The king's innocence is in part God's gift.
for he is a prophet, and he will pray for you and you shall live.
God gives Abraham, who has just failed, the task of interceding for the man he wronged. His weakness has not cancelled his calling.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that deep within the conscience a person discovers a law he has not laid on himself, which he must obey, and that conscience is man's most secret core and sanctuary, where he is alone with God (Gaudium et Spes 16; CCC 1776). The Church also teaches that those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, but seek God with a sincere heart and try to do his will, can attain salvation (Lumen Gentium 16). Abimelech is an early picture of this.

r.h: The Spirit will teach you what to say
set: Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, and thousands are gathering (12:1). He warns the disciples against hypocrisy and against fear of those who can kill only the body (12:1–7). These verses continue: the one who fears God can speak openly before others. The “synagogues, the rulers, and the authorities” in verse 11 cover every sort of court, Jewish and Gentile alike, that the first disciples came to know.
str: vv. 8–9: acknowledging and denying.
v. 10: the word against the Son of Man and the blasphemy against the Spirit.
vv. 11–12: do not worry; the Spirit will teach.
kw: To say the same thing, to confess publicly. It is the word for what the Church does in her creed.
To speak against, to slander. See the question below about the sin against the Holy Spirit.
The courtroom word, from which “apologetics” comes. The disciple does not have to prepare this alone.
vv: everyone who acknowledges me before others, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God;
A word said on earth has an echo in heaven. Jesus describes himself as a witness who speaks for those who spoke for him.
whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
A word against the Son of Man can be forgiven, and Peter, who denied him and was prayed for, is the proof (Luke 22:32). This is something else: see the question below.
for the Holy Spirit will teach you at that very hour what you ought to say.
Spoken to frightened people, not to clever ones. Many martyrs' accounts show simple believers answering judges with surprising clarity.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the disciple of Christ must not only keep the faith and live on it, but also profess it, confidently bear witness to it, and spread it, and it quotes the parallel saying from Matthew 10:32–33 (CCC 1816). Those who belong to Christ through faith and Baptism must confess their baptismal faith before others (CCC 14).

qa: What is the sin against the Holy Spirit? Have I committed it?

The Catechism explains it this way: there are no limits to the mercy of God, but anyone who deliberately refuses to accept his mercy by repenting rejects the forgiveness of his sins and the salvation offered by the Holy Spirit (CCC 1864). So it is not a particular word said in anger, or a terrible thought that comes to a troubled mind. It is a closed door kept shut from the inside. Anyone who fears having committed it, and is sorry, is showing that the door is not shut.
study: When has fear led me to say something less than the truth? What did it put at risk?
Who has shown me integrity of heart from outside my own community? What can I learn from it?

lead: Knanoitho Sunday, the fourth of the Great Fast, is named after the Canaanite woman who would not stop asking. The Sunday's many readings surround her. The Evening Gospel (Mark 7:24–30) tells the same meeting in Mark's words. Exodus 16 gives bread from heaven to a complaining people. In 1 Samuel 7, Samuel sets up a stone and says, “Thus far the Lord has helped us.” Sirach 10 warns about the beginning of pride. In Acts 20, Paul entrusts the elders at Ephesus to God. We study here the three that speak most directly to the Gospel.

Isaiah promises that God's house will be a house of prayer for all peoples. Paul cries out, “Who will rescue me from this body of death?”, and thanks God through Christ. In Matthew, a foreign mother cries out and will not go away, and Jesus calls her faith great. The key words are foreigner, rescue and crumbs. Not merit but need brings us to the Lord, and his mercy is enough.

r.h: A house of prayer for all peoples
set: Most scholars treat Isaiah 56–66 as the last part of the book, from the time after the return from exile, when the people were rebuilding and were asking who truly belonged to them. There were laws that kept some out: Deuteronomy 23:1–8 excluded the castrated and certain foreign peoples from the assembly. There were real reasons for these rules, above all the fear of losing Israel's faith and identity.

This prophet speaks a word of God that opens the door. Foreigners and eunuchs who hold on to the covenant will not be cut off. The condition is the covenant itself, which has not been loosened. What has changed is who may enter it.
str: vv. 1–2: justice and sabbath: the opening call.
v. 3: the two who feel shut out speak.
vv. 4–5: the promise to eunuchs.
vv. 6–7: the promise to foreigners, ending with the house of prayer.
kw: Literally “son of the foreign land”, a person outside Israel by birth. Here he is one who joins himself to the Lord.
A castrated man, often a court official. He could have no children, which is why he calls himself “a dry tree”. In that world, to have no descendants was to lose one's name.
Yād is “hand”, and also a memorial. God himself gives the childless man what he could not have by himself. Israel's memorial to the victims of the Shoah in Jerusalem takes its name from this verse.
vv: Do not let the foreigner joined to the Lord say, “The Lord will surely separate me from his people”;
God answers the fear before it is even spoken aloud to him. In today's Gospel the disciples speak as if that fear were true: “Send her away”.
a monument and a name better than sons and daughters;
God does not merely tolerate these people. He gives them more than they thought they had lost.
these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer;
Joy, and not merely admission. They are guests of honour.
for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.
Jesus quotes this line when he clears the Temple (Mark 11:17). Mark alone keeps the words “for all the nations”.
ch: The Church sees this promise reaching its fullness in Christ, and it hears it in the story of the Ethiopian official, a eunuch and a foreigner, whom Philip baptises as he travels home reading Isaiah (Acts 8:26–39). The Catechism says that everyone is called to enter the kingdom, which was first announced to the children of Israel and is intended to accept men of all nations (CCC 543). Lumen Gentium 13 teaches that all people are called to belong to the new People of God. The Church makes this claim without denying Israel's calling: the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29; Nostra Aetate 4).

set: Paul has just said some hard things about the Law, and he is defending it from a misunderstanding. If the Law brings about the knowledge of sin, is it evil? “By no means!” The Law is “holy” (7:12). The fault lies with sin, which uses even a good commandment for its own ends.

He writes in the first person, in the present tense, one of the most personal-sounding passages in his letters. The reading leads up to the opening of chapter 8: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
str: vv. 13–14: not the Law, but sin.
vv. 15–20: I do not do what I want.
vv. 21–23: two laws at war.
vv. 24–25: the cry, and the thanks.
kw: For Paul, “flesh” does not mean the body as bad. It means humanity on its own, weak and turned away from God. The good creation is not the problem.
Here Paul plays on the word: God's Law, and the “law” in the sense of a power that keeps working in me. The two must be told apart.
Miserable, worn out by hardship. The word cries out from the depth of the need.
vv: I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
Anyone who has tried to change a habit in the Fast knows this sentence. Paul's point is that knowing what is right does not give the strength to do it.
For I delight in the law of God in my inmost self,
This speaks well of the Law, and of the human being. The desire for good is real, and it has not been destroyed.
Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?
The question is “who”, and not “what”. Paul is not looking for a better technique. He needs a person.
Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!
The answer comes before the argument is finished. The struggle is still real in the same verse, but it has already been won by another.
ch: The Catechism teaches, following Paul, that the Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet still imperfect: it shows what must be done, but does not of itself give the strength, the grace of the Spirit, to fulfil it (CCC 1963). Baptism takes away sin, but an inclination to sin called concupiscence remains, as a struggle for us to engage in with the help of the grace of Christ (CCC 1264). So the Christian who still struggles need not think that Baptism has failed.

set: Jesus has just answered a dispute on what makes a person unclean (15:1–20). Now he goes to the district of Tyre and Sidon, on the Phoenician coast, outside Jewish territory. The passage stands between two feedings in the wilderness (14:13–21; 15:32–39), which is why talk of bread and crumbs carries such weight.

Mark calls the woman “a Gentile, of Syrophoenician origin” (Mark 7:26). Matthew alone uses the old biblical name “Canaanite”, which brings back the long history of Israel and the peoples of the land. Earlier, Jesus sent the Twelve only “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (10:6). After the Resurrection he will send them to all nations (28:19). This woman meets him before that second sending, and she anticipates it.
str: vv. 21–22: the journey and the cry.
v. 23: silence; the disciples want her sent away.
v. 24: the first answer: sent only to Israel.
vv. 25–26: she kneels; the second answer: the children's food.
vv. 27–28: her reply, and his praise; the healing.
kw: The word occurs only here in the New Testament. For Matthew's first readers it would be striking to hear the Son of David addressed by a Canaanite, using a title that many in Israel did not yet use for him.
Eleēson me, Kyrie. These are the words that have become Kyrie eleison, in our tradition Kurielaison. She uses the language of the Psalms.

A diminutive form, which may mean house dogs, or small dogs under the table, and not the street dogs of the wider world. Scholars warn against softening it too much, since the word still stings. Yet her reply makes use of just that picture of a household.
In this Gospel, Jesus says “you of little faith” to his own disciples (14:31; 16:8). He praises great faith in two foreigners: this woman, and the centurion (8:10).
vv: Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is tormented by a demon.
She says “on me”: the mother has made her daughter's pain her own. This is the beginning of intercession.
But he did not answer her at all.

This silence is one of the hardest verses in the Gospels, and many who pray know it from within. St John Chrysostom says that the delay was not to drive her away but to show her faith to all (Homilies on Matthew 52, in substance).
I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
This is not an insult to anyone. It is the order of God's plan, which begins with Israel. The covenant with Israel is kept, and it is through this that the nations will be blessed (Genesis 12:3).
But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.”
The shortest prayer in the passage. The argument seems lost. She now asks once again, on her knees.
Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.

She agrees, and then turns the picture around. She does not deny Israel's place at the table; she knows the table is big enough to have crumbs. St Augustine sees in this a great humility, and he says that it is what made her fit to receive (Sermon 77, in substance).
Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.
She came asking for a healing and goes home with this praise as well. It is a healing at a distance, like that of the centurion's servant (8:13).
ch: The Catechism names the Canaanite woman among those whose prayer of faith, expressed in words, Jesus heard (CCC 2616). Jesus teaches his disciples to pray with lively and persevering faith and with filial boldness (CCC 2610). The Church has always loved this woman because she represents all of us who had no claim to the table: the nations who have been brought in. In the Holy Qurbono we come to the table with her humility and her confidence.

qa: Did Jesus really call her a dog? Was that not cruel?

Jesus does use the word, and we should not pretend that it is gentle. Scholars read the exchange in different ways. Some note the diminutive and hear in it the household pet. Others think that Jesus is voicing the view his disciples held, to bring it into the open and then overturn it. Chrysostom saw it as a test meant to display her faith. What is beyond dispute is how the scene ends: the woman is praised and heard, and no one who reads it can think that Jesus despises her. Nor may anyone use this verse to look down on another person.
Why does Jesus say that he was sent only to Israel?

God's plan is to bless all nations through Abraham's family (Genesis 12:3). Jesus begins his earthly mission with Israel, God's covenant people, and this is not a rejection of others but the order of the promise. Paul says it in the words, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). This woman's faith gives a preview of the mission to all nations that Jesus will entrust to his disciples (Matthew 28:19).
Who is the “I” in Romans 7? Is it Paul, or the Christian?

This has been debated since the Fathers. St Augustine first thought that it described the person under the Law before grace. Later he came to apply it also to the baptised believer, who still struggles. Many modern scholars take the “I” as a way of speaking: the person under the Law without the Spirit, as Paul now sees it in the light of Christ. The next chapter stresses victory by the Spirit. Both readings agree on what matters: we are not saved by our own strength, and our help is Christ.
rite: Our Great Fast names its Sundays from Cana, from the Lord's healings and from his entry into Jerusalem: Kothine (Cana), Garbo (the leper), M'shario (the paralytic), Knanoitho (the Canaanite woman), K'piphtho (the bent woman), Samio (the blind) and Hosanna. Today's name means “the Canaanite woman”. The people repeat her cry in the Holy Qurbono: Kurielaison, Lord, have mercy. We are nearing the middle of the Fast, and on Wednesday 3 March the Cross is set up in the church. The woman's persistence is a good companion for the second half of the road.
study: Isaiah promises a place to those who felt shut out. Who feels shut out from my parish or my family, and what can I do about it?
Romans 7:15 is honest about failure. Where do I find this in my own Fast, and do I turn it into thanks to Christ or into despair?
The woman kept asking through silence and refusal. What have I stopped asking God for? Should I start again?
How would I explain “the crumbs” to a child, in a way that shows both the woman's humility and the size of God's table?
